activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Hokusai's print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well.
story:
The studio room smelled of turpentine and the chalk dust that Ms. Halvorsen refused to give up even in a building full of whiteboards. Payton taped her twelfth study to the wall and stood back beside Shania, both of them quiet while the radiator ticked.

"Ten," Ms. Halvorsen said, moving along the row of senior portfolios like someone inspecting a fence line. "Ten pieces, one theme, one statement. The college wants coherence, not a yard sale." She stopped at Payton's wall. "You have twelve."

"I know."

"Choose." Ms. Halvorsen tapped the two weakest studies with one knuckle. "These are filler. Cut them, and your series reads clean." Then she moved on to Victoria's still lifes, and Payton was left standing in front of twelve pieces of the same intersection outside the school, painted at twelve different hours of the day.

The deadline was Friday. Statements were due with the images, and hers was still a paragraph of hedge words on her phone. She had spent the whole term telling herself that the intersection was enough of a theme, that the traffic light cycling green to amber to red was enough of an argument about time, but the two extra paintings had crept in the way extra paintings do, because she liked them, and cutting them felt like cutting a piece of the day itself.

At lunch she sat with the statement draft open and got nowhere. Victoria leaned over. "Just write that you're interested in duration. That's what everyone writes."

"That's the problem. It's what everyone writes."

Shania, who was eating fries off Victoria's tray without asking, tilted her phone toward Payton. "You're moping, so I'm going to resuscitate you with art history. Did I ever tell you about Hokusai?" She scrolled to an image of a wave curling over boats, the mountain small and pale in the distance. "There's this print series, Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, from around 1830 to 1832. He called it thirty-six views."

"Okay."

"But it actually has forty-six prints," Shania said. "The first thirty-six sold so well that ten more got added after."

Payton put down her sandwich. "So the title is wrong."

"The title is the truth of when it started. The number is the truth of what it became." Shania took another fry. "I read it for that paper on ukiyo-e and I've been waiting two years for it to be useful."

Payton looked at her phone, then at the long window that faced the intersection, where the light was turning amber and a bus was deciding whether to commit. "Ms. Halvorsen said ten," she said slowly. "The colleges say ten. But the series outgrew its own name and nobody rewrote history over it."

"Don't get parochial about one teacher's rule," Shania said. "You're allowed to think past this building."

After school Payton stayed in the studio and took down the two weakest paintings anyway, the ones Ms. Halvorsen had knuckle-tapped, but not for the reason given. She laid out the remaining ten in order, hour by hour, and then set the two better extras to the side, face down, and sat with them a long while. There was a version of this decision that was pure calculation, a little utilitarianism of the portfolio: maximum coherence, minimum risk. There was another version that said the work should be allowed to exceed its container, that the container could even say so out loud.

She opened her phone and typed a first sentence, deleted it, typed it again. "This series began as ten views of the intersection outside my school," she wrote, and then stopped, because that was a lie in the wrong direction. She tried: "Ten views, submitted as ten, from a body of work that grew past its plan." That was closer. That was honest about the uncertainty, which was the thing she actually could not resolve: whether the extra paintings were vanity or whether the plan had simply been too small.

Ms. Halvorsen came through on her way out, keys in hand, and paused at the wall again. "Ten," she said, counting. "Good. You cut them."

Payton picked up the two face-down paintings. "I cut these two. The others I'm keeping at home." She heard how it sounded and kept going anyway. "The statement will say the series grew. Like the Hokusai one. Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji is forty-six prints, ten added after, when the first sold." She held one of the extras up, a view of the intersection at six in the morning, the traffic light dead against a grey sky. "This is the morning one. It's the best thing I've made."

Ms. Halvorsen looked at the painting, and then at Payton, for longer than was comfortable. "The statement had better be good," she said, and turned off the bank of lights by the door, leaving only the one over Payton's wall still burning.

Payton taped the morning painting back up, at the beginning, where the day starts, and sat down on the stool with her phone glowing against her knee, typing.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The video arrived in the group chat at eleven at night, and by the time Hannah walked to Melodie's house the next afternoon it had four thousand shares. It showed a flooded street, a man carrying a child above the water, a caption in shaky letters: SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS. Melodie's phone sat between them on the kitchen table, the clip looping again and again, and Melodie kept glancing at it the way you glance at a door someone might knock on.

"I want to post it," Melodie said. "If it's real, people should know. If it's fake, well, it's not hurting anyone." Hannah, who had shared things before and later felt the quiet itch of not knowing whether they were true, said she wanted to check first. Melodie shrugged and pushed the phone toward her, which was permission and challenge at the same time.

Hannah dragged the video into the search bar of an image engine and waited. Nothing useful came back: a page of unrelated pictures, a dog, a sunset, a grainy airport. She tried again with a different engine, the one Mr. Haddad had once mentioned offhand during a unit on propaganda, and got the same wall of noise. "It's like the engine doesn't see it at all," she said. Melodie leaned over her shoulder, chewing the end of a pen. "Maybe you can't search a video like that," Melodie said. "Maybe it only knows pictures."

That stopped Hannah. She sat with it for a moment, then thought about what she would do if she were the one cataloguing the internet: she would file pictures, because pictures were single things, countable things. A video was a river and you couldn't hand a river to a search engine. But you could dip a cup in. "Pause it," she said, mostly to herself. She dragged the playhead to the first clear frame, the man's face half-turned, and took a screenshot. Then another from the middle, the signpost above the waterline, and a third of the child's red jacket. The screenshots sat in the phone's gallery like specimens on a slide.

The first frame found nothing. The second found nothing. The third, the signpost, came back with a hit: a news article from two years earlier, a flood in a city three countries away, the same street, the same tilted sign, the same man. The article had the man's name and a quote about his neighbors. Below it, other results: the same image reposted after a different flood the following year with a different caption, and once with a caption claiming it was from a place that had never flooded at all.

"So it's real and it's fake at the same time," Melodie said slowly. "The water is real. The kid is real. The today part is the lie." Hannah scrolled, wondering how many lives a single minute of footage could have. It struck her as almost beautiful, in a cold way, the way the image had been picked up and carried and set down in a new context, like a shell moved by tides. "If we'd shared it," Hannah said, "we'd be the tide." Melodie pulled the phone back and typed a reply in the group chat, then deleted it, then typed a shorter one: it's from two years ago, different flood, checked. She hesitated over send.

"I don't want to be the fact-check police of the whole group chat," Melodie said. "Half of them will think I'm calling them stupid." Hannah understood; she had watched a boy in their class dismantle someone's post once in a tone so cerebral and so pleased with itself that the person sharing it had simply stopped posting anything at all. Being right in a way that silenced people felt like its own small failure. "You could just show them the screenshot," Hannah said. "Not the verdict. The method." Was there a difference between correcting someone and arming them? She genuinely didn't know, and she said so.

They spent another hour testing it. Melodie dragged in an older video, a clip of a crowd chanting that had gone around last spring, and paused it at three key frames, learning the rhythm of it: search, nothing, search, nothing, search, and then a match, a local news segment from a year and a half before. The chant had been about something entirely different. "It's like the video has a birthday," Melodie said, "and everyone reposting it is lying about its age." She seemed almost delighted, in the way of someone who had assumed the internet was a swamp and had just been handed a torch.

Melodie sent the message after all. A few minutes later, a reply came in: a meme about people who check things, then someone else, a boy named Matis from their seminar, posting: wait, how did you find that? Melodie typed: you can't search the video itself, so you screenshot the key frames and search those instead. Below his reply, three more people were asking, and then someone posted a screenshot of their own, of a different clip, with the words OLD, BEWARE. Hannah watched the little economy of it spread, wondering whether the tool would survive the moment, whether people would keep dipping cups out of the river or only do it while someone was watching.

Her own untouched post from three months ago, a video she had shared about a town and a fire, came back to her with an unpleasant clarity. She had never checked it. She opened the post now, thumbed to the clearest frame, and took a screenshot. Melodie watched her do it without saying anything, then slid the phone closer and said, "Start with the one on the left."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent.
story:
The garage smelled of oil and cut grass, and Kayla had spent an hour dragging traffic cones out of it while her father's old Buick sat waiting in the driveway like a patient animal. Mr. Sutton, who owned the garage and half the street's opinions, had agreed to let her practice, though he mostly watched from a folding chair with his hands folded over his stomach. She backed between the cones for the fourth time, turned the wheel too early, and clipped the rear one with a plastic crunch.

"You're looking at the cone," he said. "Look where you want the car to go."

She wanted to introspect, honestly she did, to sit and examine why her hands refused what her head understood, but the steering wheel did not care about her feelings, so she pulled forward and tried again. On the sixth attempt the Buick slid into the chalk space with a full foot to spare, and Mr. Sutton made a small sound in his throat that she chose to take as approval.

That night Jaycee's letter came, actual paper, because Jaycee had moved two towns over in March and had decided, in Jaycee's way, that texts were "too easy to fake." The envelope smelled faintly of her mother's laundry detergent, and the ink had smudged where a raindrop, or maybe a tear, had landed near the corner. The handwriting started big and shrank as it went, as if Jaycee were running out of room or courage. The last page said: My cousin drove me to Duluth last month and there was construction and everybody piled into one lane a mile early like sheep, and one guy stayed in the empty lane to the end and people leaned on their horns like he'd committed a crime, and I thought of you, because you always want to do the polite thing even when the polite thing is wrong. I looked it up after. Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent. So the horn guy was right and everybody else was just being obedient. Don't be obedient on your test. Be right.

Kayla read the letter twice, then folded it into the glovebox of the Buick, which felt like smuggling evidence into the scene of a future trial.

The test was on a Tuesday, and the examiner, a woman with a clipboard and a perfume like pencil shavings, directed her onto the highway almost immediately, where orange signs announced a lane closure ahead. The right lane had already begun to clot, brake lights stacking back through the construction zone, while the left lane stood open and gleaming and somehow accusatory. Early in her training Kayla would have merged at once, believing that patience meant signalling the moment everyone else did, that politeness and correctness were the same animal. Now she held the left lane, the letter's numbers sitting in her mind like a second passenger, and drove all the way to where the cones funneled down and the two lanes had to become one.

A pickup behind her laid on the horn, long and furious, and she felt her face go hot. Then the car in the right lane, a dusty sedan with a cracked taillight, slowed and flashed its lights, and Kayla slid in ahead of it, turn for turn, the way a zipper's teeth close. The pickup ended up three cars back, still honking at no one.

"Nice merge," the examiner said, writing something.

She would tell Jaycee about the horn, she decided, and about the sedan, and she would not pretend the choice had been easy or that she felt purely vindicated. There was something she couldn't yet name about the gap between doing the efficient thing and being hated for it, between the driver who let her in and the one who honked, both of whom were probably decent people on ordinary days. She didn't have a position on that yet, only the memory of her own hot face.

Back in the neighborhood, the examiner pointed at a curb between a hydrant and a mailbox. "Parallel park."

Kayla thought of the garage, the oil smell, the cones she had knocked over five times, Mr. Sutton's throat noises. She signalled, backed, turned the wheel late instead of early, felt the rear tire kiss the curb and adjust, and straightened out with a hand's width on either side. The chalk lines of Mr. Sutton's driveway rose in her mind so clearly she could have sworn the street smelled of cut grass.

She put the car in park and looked over. The examiner clicked her pen once and said, "Turn off the engine."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area under the curve y equals x squared, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, is exactly one third.
story:
Ms. Nair set the stack of graph paper on the front desk and announced, with the ceremony of someone unveiling a conspiracy, that they would spend the period estimating the area under a curve by counting squares. "No calculus," she said. "Not yet. I want you to suffer a little first, so you'll appreciate what's coming." A boy in the back row groaned theatrically, and Misha, beside Morgan, whispered that the suffering had begun weeks ago and Ms. Nair was merely documenting it.

Each of them drew the curve y equals x squared, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, on grid paper where every small square was one tenth of a unit on each side, so a hundred little squares made one full unit of area. Morgan laid her ruler along the parabola and began counting whole squares beneath it, then made a separate tally for the fragments the curve sliced through. The arithmetic was its own small misery. Half of this square, maybe a third of that one, her pencil hovering over slivers too narrow to name. She wrote "0.33-ish" in the margin and underlined it twice, as though conviction could substitute for accuracy.

"That's not math," Lily said, leaning across the aisle to look. "That's archaeology. You're excavating an answer."

"It's estimation," Morgan said. "It has a long and dignified history."

"So does leeching," Lily said, and went back to her own paper, where she had taken a different route, stacking thin rectangles under the curve like bricks, each one a hundredth of a unit wide. Her estimate came out to 0.3325. Morgan stared at it. Her count said almost exactly the same thing. Two methods, two people, one answer hovering near a third, and she felt the particular itch of a number that wanted to be exact but refused to say so.

When the bell rang, Morgan stayed behind, ostensibly to wash her hands of graphite but actually to stand at Ms. Nair's desk, where a textbook lay open to a chapter they hadn't reached. She recognized the elongated S at the margin of the page, the strange tall letter her older cousin once doodled on a napkin at Thanksgiving while the rest of the family argued about parking. Ms. Nair watched her look, said nothing, and began erasing the board with the unhurried patience of a woman who knew exactly what was happening and found it funny. She was mercurial in the classroom, all flash and ambush questions, but after hours she went quiet, letting students arrive at things on their own schedules.

"The chapter's not till spring," Ms. Nair said finally. "But since you're hovering."

"Is there a way to know the real answer?" Morgan asked. "Not almost. Exactly."

"There's a way," Ms. Nair said, and slid the book an inch toward her, and that was the whole of the lesson. Morgan read the notation with the slow effort of reading a language she'd only heard spoken. She did not understand most of it. But she found a worked example, and in the example, the area under y equals x squared, from 0 to 1, came out to exactly one third. Not almost. Not ish. She checked it against Lily's rectangles, against her own painstaking squares, and felt something settle that she couldn't have named before it settled: that approximation and exactness weren't enemies but collaborators, the counting of squares enfranchising the strange tall letter, giving it something to be exact about. Her grandfather, a raconteur who could stretch a trip to the hardware store into forty minutes, used to say the same thing about maps and territory, though he'd never once in his life drawn a parabola.

She found Misha at her locker and showed her the page. "The answer is one third," Morgan said. "Exactly. It's called an integral."

"One third," Misha repeated, in the flat tone of someone who had counted four hundred tiny squares for nothing. "I got point three three."

"You got one third," Morgan said. "You just got it in installments."

Misha considered this, then laughed, a short surprised bark that turned a passing freshman's head. "Fine. But next time I'm doing the tall S thing and you can count the squares." She slammed her locker, tucked the graph paper into her binder like a receipt she intended to keep, and the two of them walked out into the hallway, where the afternoon light came through the west windows in long exact stripes across the floor.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: One of Amazon's leadership principles, 'Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit', asks employees to respectfully challenge a decision they disagree with, then commit fully once it is made.
story:
Grace had wanted the veterinary clinic, and when the co-op coordinator assigned her instead to a shipping company on the harbour road, she had said thank you in an email she rewrote three times, because it seemed suddenly important to sound like someone an office would not regret taking. That was the first thing she learned about the placement, before she learned anything about freight: the way you wrote to people you didn't know was itself a kind of work. Brynn, the co-op student from the other school who sat at the terminal beside hers, composed messages the way Grace's mother arranged flowers, deliberately, with pauses.

Their supervisor, Mr. Murphy, ran the documentation team, and in the second week he gave them a real task, drafting the client bulletin about the winter schedule changes. He wanted a formal register, he said, meaning no contractions, no exclamation marks, a clear subject line, and the revised dates stated once, cleanly, near the top. Grace wrote a version full of apologies. Brynn cut every sorry and just and actually, and Grace, reading it over her shoulder, saw how much stronger it was, how the politeness she had piled on had been doing the opposite of what she intended.

The pelagic run was the problem. One of the company's routes crossed open ocean to the islands, and in Mr. Murphy's draft the change to that route appeared only in a footnote-sized clause at the bottom of the bulletin. Brynn thought the island clients would miss it. On Thursday afternoon she stood at the edge of Mr. Murphy's desk and said so, flatly, with the dates in her hand, and when he began to answer she raised her voice only slightly and said, "I'm not arguing semantics. The schedule change for the pelagic route is buried, and clients who depend on it won't see it."

Mr. Murphy listened with his pen uncapped, which Grace had come to understand meant he was deciding, not that he was annoyed. He asked one question about print costs, then said no. The clause would stay where it was; the full redesign was a matter for head office, and head office had already ruled. Grace expected Brynn to push again, to restate the argument in a different key, the way Grace herself restated arguments at the dinner table when she was losing them. Instead Brynn nodded and said, "Okay. Then I'll make the clause as clear as it can be where it is."

Afterward, in the kitchenette, Grace asked whether that had felt like giving up. Brynn rinsed her mug and said, "Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit. It's one of Amazon's leadership principles. You challenge the decision you disagree with, respectfully, and then once it's made you commit to it completely." She said it lightly, the way people repeat things they half believe, and Grace filed the phrase away, turning it over on the bus home. She was used to two versions of herself, the one who went quiet when an adult said no and the one who argued on long after arguing had stopped being useful. She had never considered that there might be a structure for the space between those two, a way to disagree and then, without sulking, to give the losing side everything she had.

On Friday they fixed the clause together. Brynn suggested the wording and Grace drafted it, and when Mr. Murphy read it he uncapped his pen, wrote a small check in the margin, and said nothing, which was his highest available praise. The clause was three lines long now, impossible to mistake for a footnote, and Grace felt a stubborn kind of satisfaction in it, the satisfaction of a thing done well on behalf of an argument that had already lost.

She thought about her father that weekend, about an argument from years ago about quitting piano, which she had won and then used so bitterly that winning had curdled into something else. She could not decide whether Brynn's principle would have helped her then or whether some disagreements were not meant to be committed to. She kept not deciding, and kept drafting emails anyway, because the placement did not wait for her conclusions.

On Monday the bulletin went out to eleven hundred clients. By ten o'clock, three replies had come in from the islands, and the first one began: "Thank you for making the pelagic change so clear." Grace read it twice, then wheeled her chair toward Brynn's terminal and held the screen so Brynn could see.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A metronome marking of 60 means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second.
story:
Arianna found the metronome on her grandmother's mantelpiece the first evening, wedged between a dish of wrapped candies and a photograph of a man she had never met. It was a small wooden pyramid with a brass pendulum and a sliding weight, and when she wound it, the mechanism stirred with a sound like a watch magnified. Her grandmother said it had belonged to Arianna's grandfather, who played the fiddle at dances before his hands went bad, and that she was welcome to it if she meant to practice. Arianna did mean to. She had borrowed the school's violin for the summer, and the audition for the youth orchestra was in September, and the piece she had chosen had a section in the middle that fell apart every time she reached it.

The passage was fast. Sixteenth notes stacked in runs that climbed and turned, and whenever she arrived at them her fingers clenched and her bow skidded and the whole thing collapsed into a noise like something dropped. She had been playing the run at speed for two weeks, convinced that repetition would eventually make it clean, and instead she had practiced the mistakes until they felt like the truth of the piece. She told herself this on the porch of her grandmother's house, mosquito screen humming beside her, while inside the kitchen the cucumbers from the garden sat in a crock and began to ferment, the whole room smelling faintly of brine and something alive.

On Saturday, Isis came out on the county bus with a tote bag full of sunflower seeds and nothing else to do. She had been playing clarinet since fourth grade and had opinions about everything, most of them delivered in short, pithy sentences that Arianna both relied on and resisted. Isis listened to the run once, all the way through, crumbs of seed shell on her knees, and then said what her own teacher had told her. "You're practicing it wrong. Slow it down. Set it to 60. That means sixty beats per minute, exactly one beat per second." She tapped the porch railing once a second to demonstrate, and the tapping was slower than anything Arianna had imagined allowing herself.

Arianna's first instinct was to argue. Playing the passage at one beat a second felt like a betrayal of the music, like reciting a poem syllable by syllable to a child, and she said so. Isis shrugged and said nothing, which was worse than arguing. Arianna slid the weight down the pendulum until the number 60 showed in the tiny window, wound the mechanism, and set the brass arm swinging. The click was metronomic in the plainest sense, a heartbeat without a body, and she put her bow to the string and played four notes per click, then two, then the full run stretched out over more measures than seemed decent. The notes were ugly at that speed, or she thought they would be, but they were clean. Every finger fell where it was supposed to fall.

Her grandmother drifted out with two glasses of iced tea and sat in the wicker chair without comment, her reading glasses pushed up into her hair. She had grown up on aphorisms, most of them from her own mother, and usually she delivered them freely, but that afternoon she only listened. After the fifth slow pass, when Arianna began to add speed by moving the weight up one notch at a time, her grandmother said quietly that her husband used to do exactly that, spend a whole evening on eight bars. She said it as if reporting the weather, and went back to her tea.

By Thursday Arianna had a system, though she was honest with herself about how much of it was system and how much was superstition. Sixty beats per minute, one beat per second, and only when a pass was perfectly clean, three times in a row, did she allow herself to move the weight. The run that had taken a week to fail at now took four days to succeed at gradually, and when she finally played it at performance tempo, the notes arrived so easily that she suspected them. It felt less like she had conquered the passage and more like the passage had always been possible and she had simply been standing in the wrong place to see it.

But she noticed something else, too, something she did not have a settled answer for. In the middle of the night, when she could not sleep, she lay in the guest room hearing the absence of the metronome, and she found she could hear the second passing, could feel a beat per second in her own pulse or in the refrigerator cycling in the kitchen. The number had gotten into her. Isis called it muscle memory, a pithy phrase that explained nothing, and Arianna thought it was more like the fermenting crock downstairs, something changing slowly in a container, becoming different from what it was without looking different. She could not decide whether that was comforting or a little frightening, that practice worked on her the way the brine worked on the cucumbers, quietly and without her permission.

On the last weekend of the summer, Garrett rode over on his bicycle to hear the piece, and she played it for him on the porch with the metronome ticking beside her at 60, the brass arm swinging, the slow click holding her steady through the fast section the way a hand holds a bicycle seat. When she finished, the pendulum kept clicking into the silence, and Garrett leaned forward and stopped it with one finger.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A LEFT JOIN in SQL returns every row from the left table, filling the right table's columns with NULL wherever no matching row exists.
story:
The printer on the second floor of the public library had been moribund for so long that Zachary felt a kind of respect for it, the way you respect a very old dog that still gets up to bark. He fed it his assignment sheet anyway, and it produced one clean page and one page streaked with grey. On the clean page, his teacher's instructions survived intact: build a database of customers and orders, then write a query that lists every customer who ordered nothing. Zachary read it four times, then went to find a table near the window.

Alayna was already there, which surprised him until he remembered she practically lived in the library over the summer, some pact with her mother about staying out of the house while the floors were redone. She had claimed the good table by spreading a calculus binder, a bag of pretzels and one shoe across it, an occupation strategy that would have been a travesty if anyone else in the building had wanted the table, which no one did.

"It's the orders I don't get," Zachary said, dropping into the chair. "Customers with no orders, they're just not there. I join the two tables and the customers with nothing vanish. Like they never existed. Which is a bad look, because the assignment literally says find them."

"Maybe they're shy," Alayna said. She slid a pretzel across the table to him like a chess move. "Maybe the join is like a party and only people with dates get in."

"That is the worst metaphor I have ever heard and also completely accurate." He pulled his laptop over and opened his practice database, the one he'd built with a customers table and an orders table, all invented names and ridiculous purchases, because if he had to stare at sample data for two hours it was going to be funny. Mrs. Vantassel had ordered a canoe. Some guy called Hal had ordered eleven candles.

He typed the join the way the tutorial had shown him, customers joined to orders, and ran it. The list came back: Mrs. Vantassel, Hal, four others, everyone who had bought something. He counted. Seven customers in the table, six rows out. A customer named Pell, who had ordered nothing, was gone entirely.

"Pell," Zachary said. "Pell is missing. This is a Pell hunt." Alayna snorted into her pretzel bag, which he chose to accept as moral support.

He sat with it. The join was doing something real, something with a logic to it, and the logic was the problem: it kept only the matches. He scrolled through the tutorial again, past the part he'd skimmed, and found a short section on a different form, LEFT JOIN, which read: returns every row from the left table, filling the right table's columns with NULL wherever no matching row exists. He read it twice, and the shape of the sentence felt almost unfair in its plainness. Every row from the left. NULL where there's no match. So the empty-handed customers weren't gone; they could be kept, marked, findable.

He retyped the query, put customers on the left, and ran it. The list lengthened. Mrs. Vantassel and her canoe. Hal and his eleven candles. And there, at the bottom, Pell, with blanks where the order should have been. He put his finger on the screen.

"NULL," he said. "Look. Pell's here, and the order columns are NULL because there's no matching order. That's how I find him, I just keep the rows where the order is NULL."

"So Pell did exist, he just stood by the snack table the whole party," Alayna said. "This is the best day of my life. Is it always left? What if I put orders on the left?"

"I genuinely don't know yet." He turned the laptop toward her, which she treated as an invitation to type, and within a minute she had reordered the query, run it, and produced a list with her own brand of chaos in it. They leaned in over the result together, and Zachary said, "Okay, so what did you just do to my data."

knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The standard tuning note is A above middle C at 440 hertz, formalized by the International Organization for Standardization as ISO 16.
story:
Emma's grandmother kept her violin in the back bedroom, under a quilted cover that smelled of cedar. Emma had asked to borrow it for the fall, since the college orchestra required an instrument and rentals cost money her parents didn't have. The grandmother had said yes over the phone, then written a letter that arrived Tuesday, because she didn't trust email. Emma read it at the kitchen table while toast cooled beside her. The handwriting slanted up the page, the ink faintly purple where the pen had run dry. "The A is true," the letter said. "I checked it against the tuner at the community center before I stopped playing. The rest you'll have to settle yourself."

On Saturday, Lincoln came over with his phone and a folding stand. He and Emma had been in orchestra together since tenth grade, and he'd offered to help her get the old instrument playable before auditions. The grandmother's house sat at the edge of town, and through the window behind the stand Emma could see the water-color of a Norwegian fjord the grandmother had painted in 1974, blue cliffs going down into darker blue. Lincoln set his phone on the windowsill and opened a tuner app.

"Give me an A," he said.

Emma drew the bow across the open A string. The needle on the app swung left, wavering, and the word "flat" pulsed in gray. She tightened the peg a little at a time, the way her teacher had shown her in the single lesson she could afford, and the needle crawled toward center. When it finally held, the app printed "440" in green.

"That's the standard," Lincoln said. "A above middle C, 440 hertz. The ISO made it official, ISO 16."

"Sounds like a bathroom code," Emma said, and he laughed, and she plucked the string again to keep the needle from drifting.

The other strings went faster. D, G, E, each one pulled toward the others by the fifths she could now hear, small beating wobbles that slowed and vanished when two strings agreed. When all four were green, she played an open scale, and the violin answered with a sound thinner than her rental had been but cleaner, like water from a well instead of a tap.

Then she took the violin into the living room, where the grandmother was sitting with her tea. Emma played the scale again, then a phrase from the audition piece, the one by the composer whose name she could never remember the order of. When she finished, the grandmother set down her cup.

"There's a fork in the sideboard," she said. "Second drawer."

Emma found it, a two-pronged steel fork, worn smooth, wrapped in a scrap of flannel. She struck it against her knee and held it to her ear. It hummed a small, lonely A. She drew her open A string against it and listened. The wobble between them was almost nothing, a breath of beating, then it steadied and the two sounds locked into one. The fork agreed with the app. The grandmother nodded once and went back to her tea, and Emma stood in the doorway between the rooms holding the fork, the vibration dying out against her fingers until it was only cool metal.

Later, on the porch, Lincoln argued that the app was all anyone needed. "Every ensemble tunes to the same note," he said. "Community center, college, whoever. If your A matches theirs, you're in." Emma turned the fork over in her hand and said she wasn't sure it was that simple. The app gave her a number, and numbers felt like the truth, the way the standardized test scores had felt like the truth about her and about Izaiah, who had scored lower and played piano better than anyone in their year. But the fork had felt like something else, an agreement between metal and wood and ear, and she couldn't say whether one was more real or only more hers. The afternoon light was already going diurnal-low across the yard, and somewhere down the road a truck ground through its gears.

"You can keep both," Lincoln said. "App for the room, fork for yourself."

"That's a cop-out," Emma said, though she put the fork in her case pocket anyway, next to the rosin. She had a week before auditions, and her grandmother's wrist was bothering her, and there was a knot of calcified rosin on the bow hair she would have to soften with alcohol and patience before Thursday. She laid the violin across her knees and played the open A once more, quiet, and listened to how long it carried out over the gravel road.

"They'll tune us with a tuner," Lincoln said. "It'll be A above middle C, 440. Same as always."

"Then I'll be there," Emma said, and drew the bow again.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: Papers posted on arXiv, the preprint server Paul Ginsparg started in 1991, are checked by moderators for relevance but are not peer reviewed before they appear.
story:
The laminated sign above the sinks read "Replication or it didn't happen," and Chase had walked past it every day since September without once thinking about it. He thought about it now, on the morning of the science fair presentations, because Rogan was at the front of the room holding a printout of a paper that Chase himself had found at two in the morning three weeks ago and sent to him with the message "this will nail your conclusion."

"According to this," Rogan said, "monarchs raised in captivity show altered migration instinct. It's basically proven." He tapped the page like a man closing a deal. Ms. Boateng, seated at the back with her clipboard, did not write anything down.

Chase's own project sat two tables over, a penurious little setup: four bean plants, a desk lamp, a borrowed ruler, a budget of roughly eleven dollars. It had cost him nothing but three weekends, and he had begun to suspect it was worth more than that. Rogan's poster board, by contrast, glowed with graphics and confidence, and up until this morning Chase had felt only a borrowed pride in it, the pride of the guy who found the source.

"And where did you find this paper?" Ms. Boateng asked.

"arXiv. It's this preprint server Paul Ginsparg started back in 1991." Rogan said it easily, the way he said everything, as though naming a thing settled it.

Ms. Boateng tilted her head. "Do you know what happens to a paper before it shows up there?"

Chase watched Rogan's mouth open and close. Around them the room had gone quiet in the way rooms do when someone is about to be wrong in public. Cordelia, perched on a stool by the window, caught Chase's eye and raised one eyebrow, and Chase looked down at his shoes because the honest answer was that he didn't know either, and he had handed Rogan the citation without checking.

"Moderators check it," Rogan tried. "For relevance. Whether it fits the site."

"That's right," Ms. Boateng said. "And that's all. It's not peer reviewed before it appears."

Nobody said anything for a second. Rogan looked at the printout in his hand as if it had changed weight. "So it could be wrong."

"It could be unreviewed," Ms. Boateng said. "Which is not the same thing, and not nothing. What would you want to see before you called something proven?"

Chase found his hand was up before he had decided to raise it. "Other people doing the same study," he said. "Like, the same question, separate labs, and it comes out the same way more than once." He was thinking of the sign above the sinks, and also of a moment last month when his own bean plant data had contradicted itself for four days until he found the lamp had been getting unplugged by the janitor. One result had told him plants didn't grow toward light. Repeating it had told him the truth.

Rogan exhaled and pulled a marker from behind his ear. He crossed out the word "proven" on his poster and, after a pause, wrote "suggests, pending replication" in cramped letters that got smaller toward the edge. "This is going to look terrible," he muttered.

"It's going to look honest," Cordelia said. She had come down off her stool without anyone noticing and was holding out her phone. "There's a 2015 study, actual journal, same finding about monarchs. Chase, I texted you the link. You can cite both and say the preprint agrees."

Chase took the phone and scrolled, and there it was, peer reviewed, boring, magnificent, with a methods section the length of Rogan's whole poster. He also found something else, something that made his stomach drop: the 2015 paper's authors were not the same as the preprint's authors, and the preprint was dated after, which meant it was a new group, an attempt, a maybe. It agreed so far. It was one voice saying the same thing once.

He raised his hand again, even though the question hour was technically over and Ms. Boateng was already reaching for the clipboard.

"Ms. Boateng," he said. "Is it plagiarism if I gave him the source? Because I did. Two in the morning, I found it, I sent it, and I told him it would nail his conclusion. So if he gets marked down, it's kind of mine too."

Rogan turned around slowly. "You're volunteering for that?"

"I'm just being accurate." Chase heard his own voice shake a little and kept going anyway. "One data point isn't a pattern. But it's a start."

Ms. Boateng looked between the two of them for a long moment, then pulled a second chair up beside hers. "Sit down, both of you. Rogan, tell us what you'd do differently next time. Chase, I want to hear about your lamp."

By the time the bell rang, Rogan had filled half the back of his poster with a plan for next year: partner up, split the monarchs, run the study at both their houses and see if the results matched. Cordelia had drawn a small crown on the corner of it and written "Team Lepidoptera." Chase gathered his bean plants, cradling the pot against his chest, and noticed for the first time that the runt of the four, the one he'd nearly thrown out in week two, had put out a new leaf overnight, leaning hard toward the window.

"Look," he said, and held it out so they could see.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech; it does not by itself stop a private employer or private company from restricting speech.
story:
I had the winning argument before I even walked into the courthouse, which is why the day went so badly, but I'll get to that. The important thing is that I'd spent two weeks on Tinker v. Des Moines and all the follow-up cases, and I could recite the concurrences in my sleep, and Mr. Addo had said, "Sadie, you're the most prepared student I've ever coached, and possibly the most loquacious," which I took as a compliment at the time and still mostly do. He had assigned me something no one else got: both sides. Petitioner and respondent. A student expelled for a post, arguing against the school one hour and for it the next.

The courthouse smelled like floor wax and old coffee, and the bailiff, a wide patient man, kept telling us where to stand as though we were pigeons. Keely was on my team for the petitioner round, and Donald was judging for another class but came to watch, which was decent of him since he'd had a migraine since Tuesday. I'd brought him a ginger ale from the machine and he'd said thanks without opening his eyes, so I knew it was bad.

Our case was simple, I thought. A student, call her the petitioner, posted a video mocking her principal, and the school suspended her, and she sued. Free speech, schools, clear line of cases. Except our fake facts had a wrinkle the teacher had planted like a landmine: the video had been removed by the website itself, a private company, before the school ever acted. So Keely, in our prep session on the courthouse steps, frowned at her notes and said, "Which one violated her rights, the school or the website?" and I said, breezily, both, obviously, and kept writing.

I want to be clear that I did not say "obviously" because I knew. I said it because Keely looked worried and I wanted her not to be, and because I had gotten very used to being the person who knew things. Somewhere in the pile of cases I had read the sentence, the actual sentence, and skimmed right past it like a pebble in shallow water.

In the first round I rose, fixed my blazer, and told the mock court that the student's First Amendment rights had been violated twice, once by the website and once by the school. The judges nodded along, and I was building speed, doing the thing where my voice gets sure and everyone lets it, when the student judge in the middle, a senior with a pen behind her ear, leaned forward. "Counsel, the website is a private company. The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech. It doesn't by itself stop a private employer or a private company from restricting speech. So what exactly is your claim against the website?"

The room went quiet in the specific way rooms go quiet when someone has been impressive in public and then stopped being impressive, also in public. Keely, beside me, wrote something and slid it over. Not the word I expected. It just said, "You've got the school part. Keep going."

So I kept going, and this is the part I'm honest about even though it doesn't flatter me: I dropped the website claim without ceremony, and the argument got better. The school was a government actor; that was the real fight; and the question of whether the suspension was justified became sharper without the dead weight of a claim I couldn't support. I lost the grand version of my case and won the smaller true one, and the judges said so in feedback, though the middle judge also said, kindly, "Never argue both directions at once. Pick the ground you can stand on."

Then, forty minutes later, I had to stand up again as respondent and argue that the school could suspend her, and everything I'd been certain of had to be set down like luggage. This is the thing nobody tells you about arguing both sides: you start noticing where your own certainty was just habit. The school's side had real ground too, the disruption cases, the fact that a thousand students saw the video in a day, and I felt a strange double vision, holding two arguments that couldn't both be right and yet each holding water when I poured it.

Afterward Mr. Addo found me on the steps eating the second half of Donald's abandoned pretzel. "You know what you did wrong," he said, and I said the website part, and he waited, because he's the kind of teacher who waits. "And?" he said. I told him I didn't know what to do about the student whose video got taken down, that the First Amendment couldn't help her there and that felt wrong to me, like free speech was a patrimony she'd been promised and then couldn't actually inherit. He said the law had other tools for some of that, and other problems it had never solved, and that uncertainty was not the same as failure. I wrote that on my hand because my notebook was inside.

Keely came out with her bag and my notes, which I'd left on the podium, because she notices things like that. "The First Amendment limits the government, not private companies," she said, in the flat voice of someone drilling it for the next round. "You taught me that today, sort of, by accident." Donald followed, squinting, holding the unopened ginger ale, and said the day's arguments had been the loudest thing his head had endured all week, but the good kind of loud. I gave him back his pretzel.

We rode home on the late bus, the one that goes past the river, and Keely asked which side I actually believed, and I said I'd tell her when I knew. She said that was a dodge, and I said it was a plan, and outside the window the courthouse shrank to a white shape and then to nothing. Keely leaned her head against the glass and said, "Next year you'll be inure to losing arguments." I said the word was "used," and she said whatever, and fell asleep before she could lose.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, the usual North American graduation processional, premiered in 1901 in Liverpool.
story:
The folding chairs had been arranged on the football field in rows so straight they looked rehearsed, and Gabriel stood at the end of the line of graduates with his gown still creased from its plastic sleeve. Behind him, Lauryn was humming something under her breath, the same eight notes over and over, and when he turned she shrugged and said it was stuck in her head, that it got stuck there every June without her ever once choosing to put it there. Gabriel listened. He knew the tune the way he knew the smell of chlorine or the sound of his own doorbell, without ever having learned it, and it struck him as strange that a piece of music could colonize a whole continent's ceremonies so completely that no one thought to ask where it had come from.

"You're going to hum that for an hour and never wonder about it," he said.

"I'm going to hum it because wondering about it would ruin it," Lauryn said, and Dimitrios, three seats up, turned around and said that wondering about things had never once ruined anything, which was the most he'd said all morning.

Gabriel took out his phone. There was no rule against it yet; the doors to the field were still closed, and the line of graduates shifted and murmured like something alive. He typed the tune's contour into a search bar, badly, got a nursery rhyme, tried again with the words he half remembered from his sister's graduation, land of hope and glory, and there it was. Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, by Edward Elgar. Premiered in 1901, in Liverpool. He read the line twice. The march was English, older than anyone's grandmother, older than the field itself, and somewhere between Liverpool and here it had become the usual processional for North American graduations, played at nearly every one, so that eighteen-year-olds hummed it without knowing its name or its country.

"Liverpool," he said out loud, holding the screen toward Lauryn. "1901."

"Shut up," she said, and leaned in to look, and stopped humming.

The discovery felt seismic to Gabriel in a small and private way, the ground under an ordinary thing shifting. He tried to tell Dimitrios, who said he'd known it was old because everything at graduations was old, the hoods and the Latin and the mace, and Gabriel said no, that wasn't it, the interesting part was that no one had decided this, or if someone had, the decision had dissolved into the tradition so thoroughly that it now looked like gravity. Dimitrios said that sounded like the start of an argument about whether customs existed in the same way tables did, and Gabriel said he genuinely wasn't sure it wasn't. Ontology, Dimitrios said, was the word for that, and Gabriel liked the word enough to forgive Dimitrios for knowing it first.

The doors opened and the line began to move. The band, eleven students who had rehearsed twice, took up the march, and Gabriel heard it now with its history attached, an English tune crossing the Atlantic and a century and settling into a June morning at a school that hadn't existed when it premiered. Lauryn walked beside him and said, quietly, "Pomp and Circumstance," enunciating it like a foreign phrase she was testing, and Gabriel said, "Number one," and she laughed into the collar of her gown.

They found their seats in the third row. Mr. Watanabe, his neighbor, his old chemistry teacher, was up on the stage with the other faculty, and when the speeches began Gabriel counted them the way he counted everything now, noticing. The principal talked about character. A student talked about the future, about how the world would test them. Gabriel listened and found he believed about half of it, and the other half he wanted to hold loosely, the way he'd hold a fact he hadn't yet checked. It occurred to him that he had two habits of mind pulling at him, Dimitrios's, which pulled everything apart to see whether it was real, and Lauryn's, which let things stay whole and beloved, and that he was going to need both, and that he did not yet know how to keep them from cancelling each other out.

When his row stood to cross the stage, Gabriel felt the usual fear, the fear that a person could only extenuate his own awkwardness so far, that there would be no explaining a stumble in front of eleven hundred people. His name was read. He shook the principal's hand, took the empty folder that would hold the diploma later, and glanced at Mr. Watanabe, who gave him the small nod he gave students who had once set a fire in a fume hood and confessed to it the same afternoon.

Afterward, on the grass, gowns unzipped, Lauryn was humming the tune again. "It's going to be stuck in there for a week," she said, and Gabriel said, "Liverpool, 1901," and she said, "That doesn't help," and kept humming. Dimitrios lay back with his cap over his face and said that neither of them had answered the real question, which was whether a tradition was a thing or just a lot of people humming at the same time. Gabriel stood there with the folder under his arm, the sun on the creased robe, and Lauryn, still humming, reached over and knocked the cap off Dimitrios's face.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one.
story:
Marcus had volunteered for the peer health program because Ms. Chowdhury said the clinic needed students who could talk to other students without sounding like a pamphlet, and because Harper had signed up first and made it seem easy. It was not easy. He stood at the counter with his notes spread across the flour-dusted surface, rehearsing how he would explain consent to a room of ninth graders, while his mother moved between the stove and the sink and pretended not to listen.

"Say it to me," Harper said, perched on the stool by the window, chin in hand. "Pretend I'm fourteen and I think I already know everything."

"Consent is when someone says yes because they want to, not because they're scared or drunk or tired of being asked." He heard his own voice go flat, like a definition read off a card, and stopped. "That's terrible."

"It's not terrible. It's just not yours yet." Harper picked up a grape from the bowl between them. "You explain things better when you're arguing. So argue with me."

They argued for an hour. Harper took the position, which she didn't believe, that asking repeatedly until someone gives in was just persistence, and Marcus kept finding the words for why it wasn't. By the time his mother set down two plates of food, he had a way of saying it that felt like his own, something about how a yes only counts if no was a real option the whole time.

The contraception part he could manage; the clinic part he could not. His script said that students who were sexually active should get tested, and every time he practiced that line, Chelsey's face came back to him from the lunch table two weeks ago, when she had said, lightly, too lightly, "Why would I get tested? I feel completely fine." He had shrugged then. He had shrugged, and it had bothered him ever since.

That night he texted her, then deleted it, then typed again. Chelsey I'm doing that clinic training. I asked the nurse the thing you said at lunch, about feeling fine. She said chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way to know whether you have one. Feeling fine doesn't prove anything. That's all. Not being weird. He read it four times before sending, because the last thing he wanted was for it to sound like an accusation, and the second-to-last thing was for it to sound like nothing.

She replied the next morning while he was making coffee: I looked it up. You're right that it doesn't prove anything. Can you come with me Thursday? I'd go alone but I'd rather not. He stood holding the kettle, watching the steam curl and vanish, and understood something about the difference between knowing a fact and carrying it to someone.

Thursday he waited with her in the clinic's small hallway, both of them reticent in the fluorescent quiet, saying little because everything important had already been said. When the nurse called her in, Chelsey glanced back once, and Marcus nodded, and that was the whole exchange. Afterward, in the parking lot, she said, "Negative. They still treated it like a normal thing to check, which was strange and also kind of a relief." She unlocked her car. "Thank you for not making it a lecture."

At the next training, Ms. Chowdhury had them do practice questions in pairs, and Marcus drew a boy who wanted to know whether he should monetize his growing TikTok following with a health channel instead of getting the actual certification. Marcus laughed and said the certification was the boring thing that made the content true, and then, when the boy asked, as if it settled everything, "But if a person feels fine, why would they bother going in?", Marcus had the answer ready and it cost him nothing to say, because he had already paid for it once at a lunch table: "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way to know. Feeling fine doesn't mean you're clear." The boy wrote it down.

Harper caught him afterward by the coat rack. "Ms. Chowdhury called your thing on consent the best in the group. She said it sounded worked out instead of copied." She pulled her scarf loose from her sleeve. "I told her you were a revisionist who rewrote everything five times, and she said that's exactly the job."

Marcus laughed, folded his notes into his back pocket, and thought about Chelsey's message still saved on his phone, and how some things he knew now he would never be sure he'd learned the right way, only that he'd carried them where they needed to go. "Come on," he said. "My mom made too much food again, and she keeps asking when you're coming back to argue at the kitchen table." He held the door.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: APY, annual percentage yield, includes the effect of compounding, so a savings rate of 4.65 percent compounded monthly is quoted as 4.75 percent APY.
story:
Megan opened four tabs before she opened the calculator, which was itself a kind of decision. The laptop she wanted cost eleven hundred dollars, and the student card in her wallet offered twelve months of financing at nineteen point nine percent, and the bank's page in the third tab was showing two numbers she couldn't stop staring at: 4.65 percent and, next to it, in a darker green, 4.75 percent APY.

She had gone to the bank's site in the first place because of Adele, who had said at lunch, "Just save for it, it's like four months of your paycheque," and then Scarlett, who was saving for nothing because Scarlett's aunt bought her things, had said something trenchant about debt that Megan pretended not to hear. The comment had stung precisely because it was accurate. Megan was seventeen, employed part-time at the garden centre, and one emergency away from a zero balance. Insolvency wasn't a word she'd used about herself before, but sitting there with the financing tab open, she thought it fit a person who owed more than she had, even if she only owed it in the future.

The two savings rates were her real puzzle. Same account, same page, one rate labeled as compounded monthly and the other labeled APY, and the APY was the bigger number. She'd assumed at first that the bank was advertising two different products and that the higher one required a minimum deposit she didn't have. But both numbers pointed to the same account, and the page said nothing about minimums. She sat with her hand on the mouse, cursor hovering over the smaller figure, and did the thing she did in math class when a problem refused to open: she made it concrete.

"If I put in a hundred dollars," she said out loud, to the empty kitchen, "the four point six five is what they use each month." She typed it, divided by twelve, multiplied it back, and watched the little answer crawl upward, month by month, each month earning its fraction on a slightly larger amount than the month before. Interest on interest. By the end of the year her hundred had grown by more than four dollars and sixty-five cents, by a hair more, and when she found the exact figure she laughed once, sharp, because it matched the darker green number to the penny. The 4.75 wasn't a different deal. It was the same deal, counted honestly, as what a year of compounding actually paid.

She called Adele, who answered mid-bite of something. "Do you know what APY means?"

"Annual percentage yield," Adele said. "It includes the compounding."

"That's what I just figured out. Four sixty-five compounded monthly is quoted as four seventy-five APY."

"Okay," Adele said, "so?"

"So the credit card doesn't quote me nineteen ninety as APY with a little green number next to it. Or maybe it does and it's buried on page nine." Megan pulled up the card's terms, scrolled, and found the disclosure the way you find a wasp in a window frame. The interest on the laptop, if she paid it off over twelve months instead of within the promotional window, would add roughly a hundred and ten dollars to the price. Interest would make the borrowed money cost more, quietly, a little every month, the same mechanism that made her savings grow, running in the opposite direction, against her.

She tried to parametrize the whole choice, because that was comfortable, putting it in rows: cost of laptop if saved for first, cost if financed, months of waiting either way, the garden centre's summer hours that would start in June and double her income. But the rows kept refusing to reduce to one number, because there was a column she couldn't fill in. The laptop was for editing video, and the video was for the portfolio due with her college applications in November, and whether a better portfolio mattered more than a hundred and ten dollars was not something a spreadsheet could tell her. She saved the file anyway and named it decision, which felt like a small lie.

Her mother came through the kitchen, looked over her shoulder at the bank page, and asked if she was opening an account. Megan said she was comparing rates, and her mother said, "Good, most people don't," and left it there, which Megan was grateful for. She didn't want to be congratulated for something she hadn't finished deciding.

She opened a new tab and typed a message to Adele: if I put my paycheques in the 4.75 account until September, I can buy it outright before the portfolio deadline. The math worked, barely, if nothing broke. That was the part she couldn't make certain, and she was honest with herself about that: the savings account could grow and the emergency could arrive in the same month, and then she'd be financing the repair at nineteen point nine percent and the whole careful structure would fold. She could hold both pictures in her head at once, the compounding in her favor and the compounding against her, and choose anyway.

She moved eleven dollars from her checking into the new savings account and set up an automatic transfer for every payday. The confirmation screen showed a projected balance for one year out, a number with a decimal she recognized the origin of. Behind her the dryer buzzed, and she went to fold the clothes while the computer held the page open, the cursor still blinking in the search box where she'd typed can i change the transfer amount later.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance, calling the 'hot hand' a fallacy.
story:
The gym at the Waverly Community Center smelled of floor wax and old sweat, and Dominic had decided, sometime in November, that it was the most honest place he knew. He was the sixth man on a rec league team that Arwa had talked him into joining, and he told everyone he didn't care about starting, which was mostly true on the days he believed it. What he actually cared about was smaller and stranger: he had begun keeping a notebook of everyone's shooting, hash marks in blue and black ink, because he was certain that some nights a player got hot and you could see it coming, like weather.

His best evidence was himself. On the third Tuesday of December he had hit four shots in a row, and he remembered it as five, and in the telling to Emma-Rose at the water fountain it had become six, and each version felt true at the time it left his mouth. That was the thing about his own memory, he had started to notice. It absconded with the misses and left the makes behind, the way a tide takes the loose sand and leaves the heavy stones.

At Friday practice the coach ran a scrimmage and put the ball in Dominic's hands to start. He missed his first two, hit his third, and then, on the next possession, Arwa passed to him again without looking, because he'd just scored. Dominic shot over two defenders and clanked it off the back rim. Arwa, though, had a habit: once she decided something was true, she fed it. He'd scored once, then twice, then a third time on a lucky bank, and after that Arwa threw him the ball every trip down the floor as though he were the only player on the court.

"Stop," Emma-Rose said finally, grabbing Arwa's jersey during a dead ball. "He's not actually hot. You just think he is."

"He made three in a row," Arwa said.

"So what," Emma-Rose said. "Coins do that."

Dominic, sweating, hands on his knees, wanted to argue, and opened his mouth to, and then didn't, because Emma-Rose was pulling her phone out of the pocket of her warmups. She was the kind of person who had a citation ready the way other people had gum. She'd read about it for a class, she said, scrolling. In 1985, three researchers, Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky, had studied basketball shooters' streaks and concluded that they were no more common than chance. She said the word carefully, working out the phonetics of "Tversky" so it came out right, the v soft and the sky hard at the end. "They called the hot hand a fallacy," she said. "That's the word they used. Fallacy."

Dominic said something dismissive about sample size, though he didn't know what a sample size really was, and Arwa said nothing at all, which was worse. He took the notebook home and sat at the kitchen table with it under the yellow light, and for the first time he counted the black ink as well as the blue. The makes made runs; so did the misses; when he laid them out in order, streaks appeared everywhere, in both directions, the way you'd expect from anything random. His system had been a museum with half the exhibits removed. He wanted to believe he'd been honest and only mistaken, but he could remember the evenings he'd thrown away the pages entirely, the nights he'd quietly redrawn a hash mark he'd smudged, always in his own favor, always in blue.

The following week Ms. Zhang, who ran the community center and refereed their games in her spare time, caught him scribbling on the bench during a timeout. She asked what he was writing and he showed her, half proud and half ashamed, and she leafed through the pages and handed the notebook back. "You know what's interesting," she said, not as a lecture, just as a remark, looking out at the court where the other team was running layups. "Either way, you play better when you think you're hot. So the question isn't only whether the streak is real." Then she blew the whistle, and he never got to hear what the question was.

He thought about that for days, and about Emma-Rose's researchers, and about Arwa's stubborn passing, and he couldn't make them all line up neatly. The streak might not be real, and still something happened when he believed in it; the belief did something the statistics couldn't see, or maybe the statistics were looking at the wrong thing, or maybe he was rationalizing again, building himself a softer fallacy out of the ruins of the first one. He wrote all of this in the notebook and then, unsatisfied, wrote beneath it: not sure. It was the first entry that wasn't a hash mark.

At the next game, in the last minute, Arwa had the ball on the wing and Dominic cut to the corner, and he was cold that night, honestly cold, two for nine, and he raised his hand anyway. Not because he was hot. Because the defender had sagged off him, and the pass was there, and his feet were set. Arwa looked at him across the pelagic blue of the floor, that deep, sea-colored paint the center had repainted the court with in the fall, and for a moment he thought she would hold it, would remember three in a row from some other night. She fired the pass instead, hard, at his chest. Dominic caught it, squared up, and shot.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Of the common disturbances to an equilibrium, a change in temperature is the only one that changes the value of the equilibrium constant K.
story:
The practice problems were on the back of the handout, and Sophia had gotten the first three right before she reached the fourth, which began with the words "the flask is heated." She wrote her answer, checked it against the key, and found she was wrong. Wrong in a way that felt total, because the key disagreed with her on every part, the direction of the shift and the final concentration and the new value of K, which she had carried straight from the previous part of the problem as though K were a fixed property of the reaction, like its colour or its formula.

The lab room smelled of vinegar from third period, and the afternoon sun came through the tall windows and lay in strips across the black counters. Sophia sat at the far station with her paper flat in front of her. Across the room Shayne was packing his bag, zipping it in that slow way he did when he wanted to be asked what was wrong.

"You look like someone stole your backpack," she said.

"Selina got a ninety-four." He buckled the strap. "I got a sixty-one. Same test. We studied together. At the same table."

Sophia turned her paper over. "Do the fourth one. The heating one. Tell me what you get."

He pulled the paper back out, read it, and worked it standing up, pen pressed against his thigh. After a minute he said, "Shift left, and K stays the same, because that's what K does. It's constant. That's literally the name."

"That's what I said."

"So we're both wrong together." He looked at the key, then at his own answer, then at the key again. "The answer key says K changed."

"You're sure you're reading the right key?"

"There's one key, Sophia."

Ms. Farah was at her desk near the door, marking with a green pen, impervious to the noise of the hallway bleeding in whenever anyone passed. Sophia did not want to go over there. Asking felt like disenfranchising herself from the small private club of students who simply understood things, and she had spent two years being quietly, comfortably enrolled in that club. But the wrong answer sat on her page like a door she had walked into in the dark.

She went over with the paper held out. "On the fourth one, if you heat it, why does K change? I thought changing concentration or pressure just shifts it and K stays."

Ms. Farah did not launch into anything. She set down the green pen, took the paper, read the fourth problem, and said, "Of the common disturbances, a change in temperature is the only one that changes the value of K." Then she handed the paper back. "Check the others you did. Look at which ones had heating in them."

Sophia returned to her station. Shayne dragged a stool over without being invited. Together they went through all ten problems on the handout, and the pattern assembled itself out of the parts: every question that only changed concentration or pressure, they had right, and K had held steady through all of them; every question that changed the temperature, they had wrong, and K had moved. The same K. Their whole method had one crack in it and every error had fallen through that crack.

"Wait," Shayne said. He had his old test out now, flattened beside the handout. He pointed at a question near the end. "This one. They heated it in the middle of the problem and I kept using the K from part b. I did that four times." He counted with his finger. "That's the whole sixty-one right there. Selina knew."

"Did she tell you?"

"She said 'watch the temperature ones.' I thought she meant the sign of the shift." He sat back. "She knew and she said six words and went to bed."

Sophia laughed before she could decide whether it was funny. The feeling in her chest had two floors to it, and she was honest enough to notice both: below, relief, because the method could be repaired, because a single fact had been missing and now it wasn't; above, something with the shape of foreboding, a first taste of how much of what she called understanding was really the luck of having been told the right sentence at the right time. She did not resolve the two floors into one. She left them stacked.

Shayne copied the sentence onto the top of his handout, word for word, and boxed it. The fluorescent light buzzed overhead and the vinegar smell had faded to almost nothing.

"Same table tonight?" he said, shouldering his bag. "Actual studying. I'll bring the problems with temperature in them, all of them, and we'll do every single one."

She slid her paper into her folder, unfoldered, creased only where her pen had pressed. "Bring two keys," she said. "I want to check the answers ourselves this time."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
story:
The parking lot behind the shuttered grocery store had the morphology of a small nation: cracked provinces of asphalt, a faded center line like a border nobody respected, and at the far end, a row of orange cones her father had set out at dawn like a disputed territory. Sadie adjusted the mirror, which showed her mostly her own eyebrow, and her father folded himself into the passenger seat with the deliberate calm of a man who had already rehearsed his own death four times in the driveway.

"Three seconds," he said. "Following distance. Minimum, according to the National Safety Council. And you add a second for every difficulty. Rain, heavy traffic, that kind of thing."

From the back seat, Marko leaned forward until his chin hovered between them. "Two seconds. My cousin's been driving for six years on two seconds and he's never hit anything bigger than a mailbox."

"We are not going to litigate traffic law from the back seat of my car," her father said, and Marko raised his hands in surrender, though his face said the appeal was merely postponed.

Sadie put the car in gear, and it lurched forward with the bellicose authority of something twice its size, startling a crow off a light pole. She had imagined this moment for months, the smooth pull-away, the casual wrist on the wheel, and instead she gave them all a small whiplash and a view of her father's hand tightening on the door handle. "Sorry. Sorry. That was the gas being a gas." She tried again, gentler, and the car rolled out across the empty lot, wobbling around the first cone by a margin that Marko kindly did not announce until they were safely past it.

"Okay, now the distance thing," she said. "How do I even count three seconds while I'm doing all this?" Her father told her to pick a fixed object ahead, a seam in the pavement, and start counting when the car in front passed it. In an empty lot there was no car in front, so Marko solved the problem by jogging ahead down the lot in his ridiculous green windbreaker, becoming, as he put it, "traffic." Sadie counted one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two, one-thousand-three as his sneakers crossed the crack, and the counting surprised her, because it was slow, slower than she expected, long enough for a whole thought to happen inside it.
