Marko swore up and down that two was plenty, and she split the difference at two and a half, watching him, and discovered that at two and a half seconds, when he abruptly stopped to tie his shoe, she had to brake hard enough that her father's coffee migrated toward the cupholder's rim.

"So three," she said, when the car had come to rest and Marko had circled around to the window to plead his case to her directly. "Three, minimum. And then a second for every difficulty." She was already glancing at the sky, where the light had gone the color of a nickel, because the first fat drops were arriving on the windshield, and the arithmetic assembled itself in her head without anyone performing it for her. "So in this, four." She said it quietly, almost to herself, and let the wipers answer her with their slow sweep. She drove the cone course again at four seconds, and the distance felt excessive and then, somewhere around the third turn, felt like the only reasonable amount of room a person could want between herself and the rest of the world.

Her father kept adding laps. Around the far cones and back, then a reverse into the space between two carts someone had abandoned years ago, then the whole course again although the rain had thickened and Marko had retreated to the car and was narrating like a nature documentary. Sadie knew what the extra laps were about. It was not about parallel parking between shopping carts. In eleven days she would be three hundred miles away at a school with its own bus system, and her father was trying to fit a year of teaching into one gray morning, one difficulty at a time. She did not say any of this. She just drove the laps, at four seconds, carefully, giving him the time.

They were stacking the cones at the end when a rusted Buick coughed into the lot and rolled up beside them, and Mr. Korhonen lowered his window with the gravity of a man delivering a verdict. "Those are my tomato cages," he said, nodding at the cones. "I've been watching you weave through them for an hour. You missed every single one." He paused, and something almost like a smile moved under his mustache. "Best driver I've seen in that lot since 1987." Her father frowned. "Who was here in 1987?" Mr. Korhonen rolled his window back up. "You were," he said through the glass, and drove off at what Sadie estimated, out of habit, to be a full five seconds behind nothing at all.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup, donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston and first awarded in 1893, is the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America.
story:
The screen door of Ms. Quinn's house had not latched in years, so everyone came in with a push and a bang, and by seven o'clock the living room smelled like the pizza boxes stacked on the kitchen counter. Game seven. Rebecca's father had claimed the good chair before anyone else arrived, and Ms. Quinn kept passing through with trays of things nobody had asked for, as if feeding people were a way of keeping her hands from shaking. Trevor sprawled on the rug with his phone held above his face. Foster sat on the arm of the couch, wearing the jersey of a team he had loved for exactly one season.

Rebecca had the letter in her backpack, still sealed in its second envelope, the one with the deadline printed in bold at the bottom of the offer sheet inside. Reply by eleven fifty-nine tonight, either school, one deposit, no take-backs. She had brought it to Ms. Quinn's on purpose, the way you bring a tooth to be pulled, and now she couldn't decide whether watching the game would make the deciding easier or just louder.

"Tied game and tied decision," Foster said, without looking at her. "That's very neat. That's the kind of thing you'd say."

"I didn't say it."

"You were thinking it loudly."

On the television the announcers were filling the intermission with history, because the game itself offered nothing yet to talk about. Rebecca half listened, then leaned forward when the camera lingered on the trophy waiting in some subterranean corridor, gleaming under work lights, handlers in white gloves circling it. She had looked it up two nights ago, at two in the morning, avoiding the letter, and what she found had beguiled her more than any highlight reel: the cup had been donated in 1892 by Lord Stanley of Preston, first awarded in 1893, which made it the oldest existing trophy awarded to a professional sports team in North America. Older than every player, older than the arena, older than the league's living memory. A thing that old still being fought over, still meaning this much.

"Did you know that thing's from 1892?" she said to the room. "Lord Stanley of Preston donated it. First awarded in 1893. Oldest existing trophy for a pro sports team in North America."

"I knew it was old," Trevor said from the floor. "I didn't know it was that old."

"It's older than the state of half these guys' grandparents," Foster said, and her father said "Sixty-seven years," apropos of nothing, meaning his age, meaning something about wanting.

Trevor rolled onto his side and held up his phone. "Message from Diaz," he said. "He says pick the city school because the games are cheaper to get into, and he says that's a metaphor." He read it in a flat voice, the way Diaz's texts deserved, and Rebecca laughed even though the laugh caught in her throat. Diaz had sent her a message too, an hour ago, that she hadn't answered: whatever you pick, pick it before the third period, don't let the game decide for you by deciding nothing while it happens. She could see the gray bubble of it when she closed her eyes.

The third period started scoreless and got meaner. A penalty, a killed penalty, a hit along the boards that made Ms. Quinn hiss through her teeth from the doorway. Rebecca took the letter out of her backpack and set it on her knees, unopened in its second envelope, and looked at it the way she'd looked at the trophy on the screen. An old thing and a new thing, and her whole future an amalgam of reasons she couldn't sort: the city school near Diaz and the cheap games, the other school with the program that actually fit, the money, the distance, the fact that one choice felt like courage and one felt like comfort and she could not reliably tell which was which.

Under the last minute the home team scored, or nearly did, the goal light flaring before the whistle came back, and the whole room surged to its feet on a play that was being reviewed above them somewhere, in some subterranean room full of monitors, by people who would decide what had actually happened. While they waited, Rebecca opened the envelope, took out the two offer sheets, turned both facedown on the coffee table, and then, before the whistle or the confirmation, turned one of them back over and began filling in the deposit form against her knee, pressing hard enough to show through the page.

The puck dropped before she finished the second line. Foster watched her instead of the game.

"You're deciding before the review," he said.

"Somebody in that room already knows," she said, and kept writing.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: A lease that says 'utilities included' may cover only some utilities; the lease wording decides which, so each utility has to be checked separately.
story:
The driving school shared a strip mall with a nail salon and a tax office, and its waiting room smelled of vinyl and old coffee. Justine had arrived forty minutes early for her lesson because the bus schedule allowed no in-between, and she had brought with her two apartment leases, one for a place on Miller Street and one for a unit above the laundromat on Cordova. She spread them across the plastic table beside the vending machine, where a laminated sign warned students not to eat in their instructors' cars.

"You're early," said Mr. Wu, who taught the evening classes and sometimes ran the desk. He set down his thermos and looked at the papers without touching them. "Homework?"

"Sort of," Justine said. "My roommate situation fell through, so I have to pick a place before the semester starts. Jasmine wants the Cordova one because it's cheaper on paper. Rose says cheaper on paper is never cheaper in real life, but she can't say why." She smoothed the second page flat. "I thought I'd work out the actual monthly cost. Total. Everything."

Mr. Wu lowered himself into the chair across from her. "Then work it out," he said, and opened his newspaper, and said nothing more, which was how he coached driving too. He believed in letting students find the ditch before he mentioned the ditch.

The Miller Street lease said six hundred and forty a month, utilities included. The Cordova lease said five ninety, utilities not included. On the face of it, Jasmine was right; fifty dollars a month was fifty dollars, and fifty dollars was two tanks of gas or a month of laundry. Justine copied both numbers onto the back of an old handout about parallel parking, and for a moment she felt the insouciant pleasure of a person who believes a problem has already solved itself.

Then she wondered what utilities included actually included, and whether both leases meant the same thing by it, and once she wondered that, she could not un-wonder it. She went back to the fine print. The Miller Street lease, four clauses deep, listed water, sewer, and trash as included, and stated in small grey type that the tenant was responsible for electricity and gas. Not all utilities, then. Some. She read it twice, then a third time, feeling the small vertigo of discovering that a phrase she had treated as a door was really a doorway with a wall built halfway across it. She called the electric company with the Miller Street address and asked what an apartment that size typically ran in the winter. The answer, roughly, was sixty to eighty dollars a month.

"Justine?" Mr. Wu turned a page of his newspaper. "You've been muttering."

"I found a trap," she said. "Utilities included only covers some of them. The wording in the lease decides which ones, so you have to check each utility separately. Electricity isn't included at Miller Street. I assumed it was." She looked at her notes. "So the real number is more like seven hundred and twenty, not six forty."

"Then your friend was wrong and your other friend was right for the wrong reasons," Mr. Wu said. "That happens more often than either of them will admit."

The Cordova lease, when she interrogated it, was worse. It named no utilities at all as included; everything was the tenant's, water included, and when she called the city to ask about average water billing for a two-bedroom, the clerk gave her a range that made Cordova's five ninety look like a disguise rather than a price. She sat back. Somewhere behind the desk a radio murmured traffic, and through the window she could see the practice cones in the empty lot, arranged in a pattern whose purpose she did not yet know.

Rose arrived at six to carpool, saw the papers, and pulled a chair over without asking. "So Jasmine loses?"

"Maybe not," Justine said, turning the handout toward her. "I called the Miller Street landlord. He said the wording is standard and he won't change it, but the super said the furnace is gas and included in a way the lease doesn't spell out, which means either the gas is free or nobody's ever tested it." She tapped the page. "I can't know that number until winter. That part stays uncertain. What I know for sure is that Miller Street is cheaper than it looks and Cordova is more expensive than it looks, and beyond that I'm guessing."

Rose read the fine print herself, slowly, mouthing the clauses. "You're being weirdly calm about not knowing."

"It's kind of interesting," Justine said. "I used to think a lease told you the price. It doesn't. It tells you part of the price and dares you to find the rest." She wondered whether everyone lived like this, whether adulthood was mostly reading documents closely and then acting anyway, and whether confidence was just solipsism that had survived an audit. She did not say any of this aloud. Instead she wrote a third column on the handout: call the super about gas, ask Jasmine to split the electric deposit, decide by Friday.

Mr. Wu folded his newspaper and stood. "Car's in the lot," he said. "Bring the papers, leave them on the back seat. A person who can read a lease can learn to check a mirror."

Justine gathered the pages, squared their edges against the table, and followed him out into the evening, where the cones stood waiting in their strange, patient geometry.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In May 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States.
story:
The moving truck smelled of cardboard and his father's coffee, and Lucas had claimed the space between the book boxes and the rolled rugs as though it were a room. Two days ago he had told Drake it didn't matter, that Kettleman was three hours away and people drove three hours all the time, and Drake had said "sure" in that flat voice that meant he didn't believe it, and Lucas had let him not believe it because arguing took more energy than he had. Now the truck lurched around a curve and a box labeled MISC slid against his knee, and he unfolded his phone to see whether anyone had texted. Nobody had texted.

They were stopped for gas outside Corning when the radio in the cab caught a news brief through the open door. His father had gone inside to pay, so Lucas heard it alone, sitting on the running board with a warm soda. In May 2023, the reporter said, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States. She said the word advisory as though it were something solid you could hold. Then she moved on to weather.

An epidemic. He turned the word over. He had thought of loneliness as a private thing, a coin you carried in your own pocket, not something a surgeon general would put his name to. But if it was an epidemic, then it was going around, then it had numbers behind it, then sitting on a running board counting your zero texts was not just his own small failure but a case of something. He wasn't sure that made it better or worse. It made it bigger, anyway.

His father came back with a bag of gas station sandwiches. "You've been quiet," his father said, which was a circumlocution for are you okay, and Lucas answered the sandwich instead of the question, saying turkey was fine. They climbed back in. Somewhere past the second range of hills, the truck's rattle settled into a rhythm, and Lucas found himself composing a message to Drake, deleting it, composing it again. He started to expatiate in the drafts, writing three paragraphs about the advisory and what it meant and how he'd been thinking, and then he read it back and hated it, because it sounded like a term paper, and Drake would rather be told almost nothing.

Here was what he hadn't told anyone, not even Milana, who could usually get things out of him: he had wanted to move. Not the leaving part, but the being somewhere his reputation hadn't already hardened around him like plaster. At his old school he was Lucas who choked at regionals, Lucas whose mother left in October, and he had started to feel that those versions of him were the only ones people could see. In Kettleman he could be nobody yet. He'd framed this to himself as brave. Lately it looked more like escape, and he could not get the two ideas to sit still long enough to judge between them. Maybe the honest thing was that he wanted both, and wanting both was what was making him silent.

He called Drake from a rest stop while his father checked the tires. Drake picked up on the fourth ring, background noise of some game or other.

"Thought you were driving all day," Drake said.

"We stopped. Hey, did you hear that thing about Murthy?"

"Who?"

"The surgeon general. In May 2023 he put out an advisory calling loneliness an epidemic. Like, an actual epidemic, in the United States." Saying it out loud, he heard how it sounded, like he was handing Drake a pamphlet.

"That's bleak," Drake said. There was a pause with a small electronic explosion in it. "You calling because you're lonely already?"

"No," Lucas said, and then, because the word epidemic seemed to demand accuracy: "Maybe. Partly."

"Milana said you were going to ghost us. I told her you wouldn't." Drake's voice had gone flat again, the voice from two days ago.

"I wasn't going to ghost you. I just didn't know what to say."

"So say that. That's what you say."

Another pause. Lucas watched his father crouch at the rear tire, tapping it with the gauge like a doctor with a knee. "It's weird," Lucas said. "I wanted to leave, and I also didn't want to leave, and I keep pretending those cancel out, but they don't. They're both just true."

"Yeah," Drake said. "That's how stuff is." Then, as if embarrassed by his own generosity: "Your new school better have a team, or you're going to be destitute. No league, no life."

"It'll have one."

"Text Milana. She thinks you're dead."

"I'll text her." He meant it this time, and he could tell Drake could tell, because the flatness lifted just slightly, the way ice does before it fully goes.

His father honked once from the cab. Lucas stood, brushed gravel off his jeans, and looked north up the highway toward a town he'd seen only in photographs. The epidemic, if it was one, would be waiting there like everywhere else, and so, he thought, might a kid on some curb with a phone and nobody's number yet. He pocketed his own phone, still warm, and climbed up into the truck as his father pulled the door shut behind him.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point.
story:
Rebecca spread the practice sheet on the kitchen table and pinned the corner with the salt shaker because the page kept curling. The question asked for the maximum of a polynomial that modeled, according to the workbook, the height of a ball thrown from a roof, and she had already written the function twice and gotten two different answers, which meant at least one of them was wrong.

She had the rules memorized. Bring the exponent down, subtract one, set the whole thing equal to zero, solve for x. Her pencil moved through the algebra and produced x equals 3. But when she substituted 3 back into the original function, the height came out lower than the height at x equals 2, which made no sense if 3 was supposed to be the maximum. She sat back and pressed the eraser end against her lip.

Neil came through the back door without knocking, the way he had since they were nine, holding a bag of chips and his own worksheet. "Harper's exam is Thursday," he said. "You doing the throwing problems?"

"One of them hates me." She turned the sheet so he could see. "I got 3, but the ball's higher at 2. So either the ball is lying or I am."

Neil dropped into the chair across from her and ate chips while he read. He was not perspicacious in the way teachers praised, not the student who saw the trick instantly, but he was stubborn, and stubbornness got him through most things eventually. He tapped her second line of work. "You dropped a negative here. Minus two x squared, so the derivative is minus four x, not plus."

She checked it against the first line. He was right. She copied the corrected version below, set minus four x plus twelve equal to zero, and got x equals 3 again, but this time when she substituted, the height came out above everything around it. Still, the earlier wrong answer had unsettled her. "But why do I trust this?" she said. "Last time the algebra looked just as clean and it was garbage."

"There's the graph paper," Neil said. He pulled a sheet from his backpack and drew axes, plotted the curve from a table of values, the parabola arcing over and coming down. Then he took the ruler from the drawer by the stove and laid it along the curve at the top, tilting it until it sat flush against the arc the way a shelf would sit against a hill. At the peak, the ruler lay level.

"That's the tangent," he said.

She looked at the ruler, then at her page, where the derivative at 3 evaluated to zero. The pencil marks and the ruler were saying the same thing in two languages, and she felt something click into place that she could not yet put into words. "So the derivative at a point equals the slope of the tangent line right there. That's why zero means the top. The line's flat."

Neil slid the ruler to the left along the curve, where the arc climbed steeply, and then down the falling side. The slope of the ruler tilted up one way and down the other, and her computed derivative at those points, when she worked them out on the margin of the sheet, gave positive numbers on the climb and negative numbers on the fall. She wrote the values along the curve in small print, like annotations on a map.

Aliza texted a photo of her own attempt an hour later, after the two of them had moved to the porch with the last of the chips. Her answer was x equals 3 with a different function entirely, and she had ascribed her success to a formula she'd found online, a shortcut she couldn't justify. "It gave the right answer," her message read, "so I'm not asking questions."

Rebecca typed a reply and deleted it twice. She wanted to say that the answer wasn't the part that mattered, but that wasn't quite honest either, because Thursday was a graded exam and the answer did matter. What she actually believed was closer to this: the shortcut and the ruler were both roads to the same place, but only one of them would hold up on a question she'd never seen before. She sent, "The ruler check takes two minutes. Bring one Thursday." Then she set the phone face down, took the graph paper back from Neil, and laid the ruler against the curve one more time at the peak, turning it slightly, watching for the exact angle where it touched and nothing more.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: On a stage in the round, the audience sits on all sides, so the director must keep actors moving so no section only sees their backs.
story:
The gym had been promised to the drama club for three weeks, and on the first Monday of rehearsals Violet found it transformed: the janitors had stacked the bleachers back and set chairs in a rough circle on the floor, four deep, around a square of taped linoleum in the center. She stood at the edge of the square holding her binder of notes and understood, slowly, that everything she had planned in the empty hallway outside the library was wrong.

"It's in the round," Juan said, dropping his bag on a chair in the second row. "The whole audience sits on all sides. Ms. Cruz says it's a gift."

It did not feel like a gift. Violet had blocked the one-act on the image of a proscenium, an invisible fourth wall with the audience somewhere beyond it, and her diagrams had the two actors facing one direction for entire pages of dialogue. She had even printed them. Now she looked at the chairs on all four sides and pictured the families who would sit behind the taped square, behind the actors' backs, for the whole quarrel scene, and she felt her stomach drop in a way that had nothing to do with stage fright.

Lorelei arrived with two coffees and a hoodie she refused to take off even in the heat of the gym. "So walk us through it," she said, handing one to Violet. "You're the director. We're your puppets."

"You're not puppets," Violet said, and then, because she was honest even when it cost her, "but I did kind of treat you like puppets when I drew this." She showed them the diagrams, the arrows, the neat X's and O's. Juan studied his page for a long moment and then turned it upside down as if the problem might be orientation. Lorelei laughed, but not unkindly.

They tried it anyway. Violet set Juan and Lorelei on their marks, facing what would have been the audience, and ran the first page. From her own seat behind them, in the north section of chairs, she watched the backs of two heads exchange words she could not fully hear, their faces appearing only in quick quarter-turns. She stopped them. "Okay," she said. "That's unwatchable from here."

"So turn us," Juan said. "Move us around."

She began to experiment. She learned that if she kept them circulating, slow rotations through the quarrel so that each section of chairs got the actors' faces in turn, no side was starved for long. It was harder than it looked; the movement had to be motivated by something in the scene, a grab of the wrist, a retreat to the far edge of the square, or it read as mechanical, actors on a lazy Susan. She scrapped her diagrams page by page, tearing them out of the binder and letting them collect on the gym floor, which felt simultaneously like progress and like destruction.

Ms. Cruz came through at the end of the first hour, ostensibly to check that nobody had climbed the equipment racks. She watched one run of the quarrel from the west side, moved without comment to the east side, watched it again, and said only, "Better from there." Then she left, and Violet understood that the compliment contained its opposite.

The trouble came on Wednesday. Lorelei had found a choice she loved, a long stillness in which she simply stood and let Juan circle her, and it worked from three sides of the room and not at all from the fourth, where her face went flat and lost. Violet asked her to rotate through the stillness, one slow turn over the course of the speech, and Lorelei refused. "It dilutes it," she said. "You're directing the audience and not the scene. It's a specious kind of fairness, making everybody see everything."

"Then a quarter of the room sees nothing," Violet said.

"Maybe a quarter of the room should."

They stood in the middle of the taped square while Juan sat in the chairs pretending to read his script and obviously listening. Violet could have pulled rank; it was her one-act, her name in the program under the word director, and under the duress of the Friday deadline the authority would probably have held. She also knew that Lorelei was not denigrating her instinct, was not calling it stupid; she was arguing, with real conviction, that a director's first loyalty was to the moment and not to the seating chart. Both positions were true in the way that two hands pulling a rope in opposite directions are both really pulling.

"Half a turn," Violet said finally. "You turn through the speech only until you face the fourth side, and you hold there for the last three lines."

"Facing away from the biggest section."

"Facing away from the biggest section, at the moment you say the thing you've been avoiding. Let them watch your back for the admission. That's a choice, not an accident."

Lorelei considered it, jaw tight, and then nodded once. Juan stood up from the chairs and said, "Then I'm behind her, so that side gets my face." He said it lightly, but it solved the geometry, and Violet wrote it into the margin of her script with a pencil she then had to hunt for under the bleachers.

Friday night, the chairs filled. During the quarrel, Violet stood against the far wall by the water fountain, out of sightlines, watching sections of the audience instead of actors. The faces turned where she had taught them to turn. And when Lorelei made her half rotation and stopped, back to the biggest section, delivering the last three lines into the empty air above the east chairs, some part of Violet still did not know whether it was the best choice in the play or a compromise she had dressed up as vision. She watched Lorelei's shoulders rise with the breath after the final line, and behind her, Juan reached out and turned off the work light that stood in for the ending blackout.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Herman and Chomsky's second filter is advertising: outlets that depend on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away.
story:
The envelope was waiting on Robert's desk when he got to the newspaper office on Tuesday, propped against the monitor like a bill he already knew he couldn't pay. It was from Halvorsen's Home & Garden, which had bought the back page of The Beacon for three years. Robert had written the story himself, four hundred words about how the store's "spring clearance" marked up lumber two weeks before discounting it, and he had checked the numbers twice. He slit the envelope open with a letter opener that belonged, he supposed, to the school.

"Dear Editor," he read aloud, because Jerry insisted on hearing it. "We were disappointed by your recent article, which we feel misrepresents our business practices. Unless a correction is printed, we will be withdrawing our advertising for the coming year. Sincerely, Dean Halvorsen." The office smelled like toner and the burnt coffee someone had left on the hotplate since morning. Outside, a maintenance crew was running a leaf blower across the quad, its drone coming through the single window in waves.

"Print a correction," Jerry said. He was layouts editor and spoke about most things the way he spoke about margins. "One advertiser. We'll find another."

"He's a quarter of our budget," Robert said. "There is no other. There's him, there's the pizza place, and there's whatever the school gives us for paper." Jerry went noncommittal, shuffling proofs that didn't need shuffling, and Robert sat down without taking off his coat.

Branden came in twenty minutes later with his backpack still on one shoulder and a photocopy in his hand. He was the one person on staff who took a media studies elective, and he treated the rest of them like missionaries treat the unbaptized. "I looked it up," he said. "This is a thing. Herman and Chomsky. They wrote about how the money works in news." He put the photocopy on the desk between them, and Robert read enough of it to understand that his problem had a shape, that it wasn't just Halvorsen being thin-skinned.

"Say the part about ads again," Robert said.

"Advertising," Branden said, tapping the page. "Their second filter. Outlets that depend on advertisers' money have a reason to avoid coverage that drives those advertisers away." Jerry, from the corner, said "filter" like it was a word Branden had invented on the bus, but Robert was quiet, because the sentence described the room he was sitting in with uncomfortable precision. He had always thought of The Beacon as independent the way he thought of himself as independent, which was to say nobody had tested it yet.

Ms. López, whose classroom was down the hall and who advised the paper without ever touching it, came by at the end of the day for the keys to the cabinet. Robert told her the whole thing, the story, the letter, the number, and she listened while she sorted the keys onto their hook. "When I was in journalism school," she said, "we all thought the pressure would come from above, from some despot of an editor. It usually comes from the billing office." She didn't tell him what to do, which he understood was her way of telling him it was his to do, and she left with her mug under her arm.

He worked on it that night at the desk in his bedroom, where the radiator ticked and his mother watched television one floor down, her laughter rising through the floorboards at odd intervals. He tried to write the correction Halvorsen wanted and couldn't, because every sentence calcified into something he didn't believe, an apology wearing the clothes of a fact. Then he tried to write a full-page editorial about Herman and Chomsky and couldn't do that either, because it read like a boy discovering gravity and announcing it. The truth, he decided somewhere after eleven, was smaller and harder to hold: the story was right, the money was real, and both of those things were going to be true at the same time no matter what he printed.

On Thursday he called Dean Halvorsen from the office phone, with Jerry and Branden standing close enough to hear both halves. He offered to run a follow-up, a fair one, giving the store room to explain its pricing, if the ad stayed. Halvorsen said he'd think about it, and then, in a quieter register, asked whether the kid who wrote the original had even been inside the store. Robert said he had, twice, and had bought a tape measure there. There was a pause long enough that Robert could hear the store's PA system in the background, calling someone to register two.

The follow-up ran the next week, and so did the ad, and Robert didn't fully know whether that was a win, because the follow-up was honest and the deal was not clean, and he had spent the whole edit feeling the shape of the second filter in his own hands. Branden taped the Herman and Chomsky page above the coffee station, where it slowly curled from the steam. On Friday afternoon Jerry looked at the tape, looked at Robert, and said, "So next year we find advertisers who don't care what we write."

"Nobody doesn't care," Robert said, and turned the hotplate off.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Alicia had agreed to meet Nika at the rink because neither of them could think of anywhere else, and because Nika had said, in the group chat, that she was actually good at skating, which Alicia suspected was a lie and found herself hoping was true. She arrived early, which was a mistake, because arriving early left her forty minutes to stand by the skate rental counter and think. On the phone last night, Rosemarie had tried to help. "Don't spiral," Rosemarie had said. "Also, there's this thing you should know. A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found what they called the liking gap. After a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company." Alicia had written it in her notes app under a heading she now found embarrassing: EVIDENCE.

She rented skates and watched the Zamboni make its slow blue circuits. The rink had two moods and she could never decide which she preferred. On the far side, a speed skating club trained in grim silence, their blades hissing like something industrial. On the near side, under the string lights, there was a snack bar and a playlist and eleven-year-olds playing tag, and the whole corner had a hedonistic glow about it, sugar and noise and nobody keeping score. Alicia had spent most of her life wanting to be the sort of person who trained on the far side. Tonight she was going to be a person on the near side, holding hands with someone, and the thought made her throat tight.

Nika arrived at 7:04, red-faced from the walk, hair still carrying snow. "I'm late, I know, the bus lied to me. Also I have to tell you something immediately, before we skate, because I'll lose my nerve." She took a breath. "I'm not actually good at skating. I'm bad at skating. I said I was good because you seemed like the kind of person who'd respect skill, and then I panicked."

"Wait," Alicia said. "I can't skate either. At all. I told you I 'dabbled.'"

"You said you dabbled."

"I've been on ice twice. Both times holding a wall."

Nika laughed so loudly that a woman at the rental counter looked over. They stood there grinning at each other like idiots, and then they got their skates and shuffled out to the learner's corner, where Ms. Park, who taught the Saturday morning class and seemed to know everyone under twenty in the neighbourhood, was lacing up a small child's helmet. "Falling is a skill," Ms. Park told the child, not unkindly. "Learn to do it on purpose and you'll stop fearing it by accident." Alicia heard it and did not take it as advice, because it wasn't meant as advice, but it sat in her anyway.

The first ten minutes were a catastrophe. Nika went down twice; Alicia went down once and took Nika with her the second time; a nine-year-old in a hockey jersey offered them both a gloved thumbs up. But somewhere after that, the catastrophe became the whole point. They invented a system where the worse skater at any given moment held the other's sleeve, and they got good at arguing about who was worse, and Nika described her chemistry teacher in brutal detail, a man who had spent four consecutive lessons on polymers, drawing the same chain of little circles on the board until the whole class could reproduce it asleep. "He kept saying, imagine a single unit, a monomer, all alone, useless, basically. Then he'd draw the arrow. Monomer, monomer, monomer, boom, plastic. Like the chain was the moral of the story." Nika wobbled, caught Alicia's arm, and added, "I thought it was boring. Now I think about it a lot, actually. How things that can't do much alone turn into the thing holding everything together."

They skated until the session ended. At the door, in the overheated lobby, there was the terrible moment Alicia had been dreading since Tuesday: the goodbye. Nika said she'd had fun, but Alicia heard it the way she heard everything, as a form people filled out, and she said "yeah, me too" in a voice that came out flat, and then Nika was walking toward her bus and Alicia was walking the other way with her boots in her hand.

The walk home was twenty minutes of replay. The moment she'd talked too long about her brother. The moment she hadn't laughed at Nika's joke fast enough. She assembled the evidence item by item, and it all pointed one direction, toward the conclusion that Nika had endured the evening the way you endure a dentist. Then, somewhere past the corner with the broken streetlight, Alicia stopped and stood in the cold and did something she was embarrassed to do in public, which was think on purpose, deliberately, the way she did before an exam, refusing to let the verdict arrive on its own. She took out her phone and opened the notes app, and there was her own heading, and Rosemarie's fact, and she read it again after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company, and noticed that it said usually. It didn't promise anything. It didn't tell her what Nika felt. It told her only that the tape in her head was an unreliable instrument, that the reel of her own failures was not data.

She stood under the broken streetlight for another minute. Then she typed: "Okay, confession. I can't skate and I was terrified the whole time and it was still the best night I've had in months. Also I'm bad at goodbyes, which is why I just said 'yeah, me too' like a robot." She read it four times, deleted "like a robot," put it back, and sent it before she could cogitate her way out of it. The reply dots appeared almost immediately.

"OH THANK GOD," Nika wrote. "I've been walking to my bus composing a whole speech about how you clearly regretted everything. Come back Saturday. I want to beat the nine-year-old at tag."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
The marquee lights still read seven forty-five when Hailey got there, though it was seven fifty-two, and she decided not to mention it because Hussein was already standing under the word NOW showing with his hands in his pockets like a boy posing for a photograph he didn't want taken. He had asked her out on Tuesday, in the parking lot, with a pugnacious little jerk of his chin, as if he expected to be refused and intended to argue the point. She had said yes mostly to find out why he'd braced himself.

They bought tickets for a movie neither of them had heard of, and it turned out to be mostly fog and subtitles, and halfway through she realized she could not remember a single thing that had happened in the first half. What she remembered was the exact sound of his jacket sleeve against hers on the armrest. Afterward, in the theater's little café, over two watery hot chocolates, the talk that had limped along before the film died entirely. He asked about her classes. She asked about his job at the garden center. Both answers were true and both were useless, and she sat there wondering whether this was what everyone meant by chemistry, the absence of anything to say while someone attractive said nothing across from you.

"So," Hussein said, and turned his cup a quarter turn, and turned it back. "There's this thing. A psychologist, Arthur Aron, did a study in 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions, and the questions got gradually more personal as they went. By the end they felt closer than pairs who just made small talk." He said it fast, the way you confess to having practiced something.

"Where did you read that?"

"Online. Months ago. I kept it." He pulled out his phone, showed her the list, and she noticed his thumb hovering over the screen as though she might grab it. "I'm not saying it's, like, magic. I'm saying we have forty minutes until your bus and nothing else."

She wanted to say that was the most romantic thing anyone had ever proposed to her and also possibly the saddest, and she could not decide which, so she said, "Number one."

He read it. "Given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest?" He thought, really thought, and said his grandmother, who had taught him to cook and who had died in March, and he hadn't told anyone at school that, he said, because what was there to say. Hailey answered with a name that surprised her, a poet she'd loved at fourteen and abandoned, and found herself explaining why she'd abandoned him, which required explaining what she'd been like at fourteen, which required more honesty than the entire fall semester.

They went on. The early questions felt like stepping stones, safe and dry, and then somewhere around the teens the water rose. She noticed that the order mattered, that she could not have answered question twenty at question five; the small ones had built something the bigger ones could stand on, which made her wonder whether closeness was a thing you could engineer, or whether the questions only uncovered what was already there and would have come out anyway, given enough bad movies. She asked Hussein this, between questions, and he said, "Both, probably," and then, "Your turn."

He had a want of his own; she could see it now. He wanted to know if she liked him, and he was using the questions the way you use a ladder, careful rung by careful rung, glancing up between each one to see whether she was still there. When she asked whom he most admired, he said his older brother, who had come out two years ago to their father and stood in the doorway doing it, and Hussein said he'd sat on the stairs listening and thought, that, that is what brave looks like. He said he'd wanted to be that brave about something ever since and hadn't found his something yet.

She felt the word solipsism rise in her then, a word from English class, the fear that she was the only real thing in the world, everyone else just weather, and here was this boy across the table being unmistakably real, with a dead grandmother and a brave brother and a list on his phone, and she thought the study might be less about the questions than about the taking of turns, the agreement to stand still and be asked.

Question thirty-four asked what she would most regret not doing if she died, and she started to answer twice and stopped, and Hussein waited, not checking his phone, and she thought that his waiting might presage something, or might be nothing, patience is not a promise.

"Ask me the last one," she said, "but don't read it yet. I want to see your face when you do."

He scrolled, looked up at her, and set the phone face down on the table between their cups.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Readers usually detect an unreliable narrator through contradictions, such as other characters' words or the events themselves not matching what the narrator claims.
story:
Leah arrived at the book club early enough to claim the corner chair, the one beside the window where the November light fell flat and gray across the library's small meeting room. She set her copy of The Lamplighter's Daughter on the table, its margins crowded with orange sticky notes, and began to collate them in the order the events happened, not the order the narrator told them. That was the trick she'd stumbled on three nights ago, rereading until midnight: the narrator, Marta, said one thing, and the story around her said another.

Ms. Chan poured coffee from the dented thermos she brought every second Thursday and slid a cup toward Leah. "You've been busy."

"A little." Leah fanned the notes across the table like an archipelago, small orange islands, each one a page number and a sentence copied out in her cramped hand.

Nadia came in last, breathless, scarf still wound to her chin. She dropped into the chair across from Leah and pulled out her own copy, pristine, its spine uncracked. Nadia always spoke first at these meetings, and Ms. Chan always nodded at whatever she said, and Leah had spent two months deciding whether that was worth resenting. Tonight she wanted the nod herself, though she hadn't admitted that to anyone, including herself.

"So," Nadia said, "Marta. Obviously she's an unreliable narrator."

"Obviously," Leah said, and waited.

"I mean, the whole thing is her trying to make herself look better. You can just feel it." Nadia turned a page at random, a performance of engagement. "Her tone. The way she talks about her sister."

Leah's hand went flat on the table. She had forty-one sticky notes that said it wasn't about tone at all, and she felt the tectonic shift of an argument gathering under her ribs, but she also knew Nadia had wanted to lead this discussion since the book was chosen, had told everyone at lunch she had "a theory." Leah looked at her notes, then at Nadia's clean pages, and chose her words the way she'd choose footing on ice.

"Feel it how?" she asked.

"You just do. The sister seems too perfect, and Marta's always complaining about her, so."

Ms. Chan settled into her chair with her own copy, which was as thumbed as Leah's. "Let's test that. Where does the book actually contradict her?"

The room went quiet. Nadia's fingers moved on her uncreased page. "It's more of an overall impression," she said, and Leah felt the truth arrive before Nadia finished the sentence: she hadn't read past chapter four.

But Leah didn't say that. Instead she picked up her first sticky note and read it aloud. "Page twelve. Marta says her sister never wrote to her after she left. Page fifty-eight, the letters are in the drawer, fourteen of them, unopened." She laid the note down. "Page ninety-one. Marta says she was the one who put out the fire. Page one-thirty. The neighbor's account says she was standing in the road while the apprentice did it." She kept going, note by note, and the pattern emerged the way a photograph emerges in developer fluid, every place where another character's words or the events themselves refused to match what Marta claimed.

"That's why we don't trust her," Leah said. "Not the tone. The contradictions."

Ms. Chan was leaning forward now, and Leah realized she had stopped watching for the nod. Nadia had gone very still.

"I marked every one," Leah went on, slower now, because something was snagging in her. "Every single contradiction. And here's the thing." She held up the last note, the one from page two hundred and six, which she had written at one in the morning and had not decided what to do with. "The apprentice, the one who saved Marta from the fire and never told anyone, is the only person Marta never contradicts. She lies about her sister, about the fire, about the money. About him, she only ever says one thing, that he left. And the book never shows us anything different."

"What are you saying?" Nadia asked, and her voice had lost its performance entirely.

"I'm saying I don't know. Either that part is true, the one thing she never dressed up, or it's the biggest lie in the book, and the author left it clean on purpose so we'd fight about it." Leah looked at the archipelago of notes, all that evidence, and at the one blank space in the middle of it. "I collated everything she got wrong. I can't collate what she didn't say."

Nadia pulled her chair around to Leah's side of the table, sat down, and reached for the stack of notes. Her copy of the book stayed shut on the table behind her.

"Start from page twelve again," Nadia said. "I want to see all of them."

Ms. Chan refilled both their cups and turned to page fifty-eight.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Congress can override a US president's veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate.
story:
The council chamber smelled like floor wax and burnt coffee, and Violet counted the empty seats before she counted anything else. Nineteen chairs behind the curved dais, twelve of them filled, the rest abandoned by council members who had apparently decided the rezoning agenda could proceed without them. She and Mickael and Nolan sat in the fourth row with a printed copy of the ordinance and a bag of gas station candy, because the city had been debating the shelter's buffer zone for three meetings now and the meetings ran long.

They had come for the local ordinance, but the thing Violet actually wanted was two thousand miles away, in Washington, where the expanded indigent housing voucher bill had come back from the president's desk unsigned. Nolan had printed the whip count that morning and folded it into quarters like a letter he intended to deliver personally. "He vetoed it," Nolan said, not for the first time. "He actually vetoed it."

"He did," Mickael said. "Saying it again won't un-veto it."

At the front, a councilwoman moved the ordinance out of committee with a sentence full of the vernacular of municipal government, first reading, second reading, public comment, and Violet wrote the words down because the sequence itself was the lesson. Draft, committee, debate, vote. It was the same shape as the thing in her pocket, the same architecture at a different altitude. The clerk read the ordinance text aloud, and the language had changed since the draft she'd read online; the buffer distance had shrunk from a thousand feet to three hundred, and someone had inserted the word "shall" where "may" used to be.

Nolan leaned across Mickael to talk to her. "The House passed the voucher bill before with two hundred and sixty votes. So the veto doesn't kill it. Congress can override a president's veto with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate." He said it like a fact he had guarded all day and was now setting down.

"That's two hundred and ninety in the House," Violet said. She had done the division on the bus, twice, because she distrusted her own arithmetic when it mattered. "Two-thirds of four hundred thirty-five. We're thirty short."

Mickael, who wanted to be an accountant and treated every dispute like a ledger, took the folded whip count out of Nolan's hands and smoothed it on his knee. "But that two-sixty was the vote on passage. Some of those people voted yes because they knew the president would veto it. Free yes votes. Safe yes votes. An override is different. An override has to survive being seen." He began marking the list, a small x beside each likely defector, and Violet watched the count come apart in his hands, from two hundred and sixty to two hundred and forty to something he wouldn't say out loud.

The spring before, in Ms. Haddad's classroom, Violet had presented the veto as a wall, final, simple, and Ms. Haddad had asked her one question in front of everyone: "So what is a veto for, if it can be undone?" Violet had stood at the whiteboard without an answer, and the silence had lasted long enough to be educational. She thought of it now, the way you think of a wrong turn hours after you've taken it. Nolan believed the wall was coming down because it had to; Mickael believed the numbers were the numbers and hope was not a vote. Both of them had the same page in front of them and were reading different documents.

"Public comment on item seven," the clerk said, and Violet stood up before she had fully decided to. She had signed the card an hour earlier intending to talk about the buffer zone, the shrunk distance, the shelter's residents who walked past her bus stop every morning, and when she got to the microphone that was what came out, plain sentences, the "shall" and not the "may," the three hundred feet. A councilman with reading glasses asked her a question about parking flow that she could not answer, and a woman two rows back said, "Ask her about the snow," which got a laugh from the galley, and which nobody explained.

Afterward, outside, under the yellow lamps of the parking structure, Nolan and Mickael were still at it. "If they get it to the Senate," Nolan said, "the Senate has to do it too. Two-thirds there as well. Both chambers. That's the whole rule."

"I know it's the whole rule," Mickael said. "I'm telling you the House is where it dies. You can't get to two-thirds of both when you can't get to two-thirds of one."

Violet took the whip count back and looked at the x marks, at the unmarked names, at the margin where Ms. Haddad's question was still waiting to be answered. A veto wasn't a wall; it was a price. It made a yes vote cost something, and most votes were cheap, and nobody could say yet which thirty of the two hundred and sixty would pay. "I don't know if it passes," she said. "I know it's not dead. Those aren't the same thing and I'm tired of pretending they are."

Nolan held out his hand for the paper. "So we count again Thursday."

"Thursday," Mickael agreed, and folded the list back into quarters along its worn creases.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: A 2005 study by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues found that email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness.
story:
Amy sent the email at 11:40 on a Tuesday night, after her shift at the garden center had gone badly in every small way a shift could go. The new manager, whom everyone called by his last name, Deckard, had left a note taped to the register about the watering schedule, and Amy had replied from her phone with what she thought was obvious sarcasm: "Great, I'll be sure to water the cacti twice as much, since that worked so well last week." She signed off with a winking face and went to sleep feeling lighter than she had all day.

On Thursday, Deckard called her into the back office, which smelled of fertilizer and old coffee. He slid a printout of her email across the desk and asked, in a voice that was quiet rather than angry, whether she had a problem with the way he ran the place. Amy stared at the paper. The winking face looked, in twelve-point font on a manager's desk, like something a child would send. She said no, that she'd been joking, and he nodded slowly and said he'd take her word for it, but that in writing he couldn't hear her smile. She spent the rest of her shift ringing up petunias and feeling the shape of the conversation she hadn't managed to have.

That night she typed "emails come across wrong" into her laptop, half expecting nothing useful. Instead she found a study from 2005 by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and others, which found that email writers overestimate how well readers will pick up their intended tone, such as sarcasm or seriousness. She read the sentence twice, then a third time. The study was old enough that it had been sitting there, published and waiting, for her whole life. She caught herself arguing with it anyway. She knew her own voice, knew how obvious the joke had been. Then she remembered Deckard's face, and the printout, and the argument went quiet.

She drafted an apology that Friday, and this time she treated it like the structured essays Ms. Haile had drilled into them senior year: a clear opening that named what she was sorry for, a middle that explained without excusing, a close that proposed something concrete. She wrote that she would keep future emails plain and factual, and that if she had a concern about the schedule she would raise it in person. Reading it back, she disliked how stiff it sounded, how little of her it contained. It felt like wearing someone else's uniform. She sent it anyway, and then closed the laptop before she could soften it with a joke.

Mischa, who worked weekends at the café two doors down, looked at the apology draft on Amy's phone during their break and made a face. "It's so formal," Mischa said. "You're a person, not a customer service bot." Ronan, who had transferred from another branch and was eating fries on the curb between them, disagreed before Mischa had finished. "It's his name on the schedule," Ronan said. "You write like the situation is, not like you feel." They went back and forth, Mischa insisting that sincerity needed some slack in it, Ronan holding that respect was the slack, and Amy sat between them realizing she agreed with both of them a little, which was an uncomfortable place to sit.

She thought about determinism for a moment, the idea she'd half learned in a philosophy elective: that every outcome flows inevitably from what came before. If that were true, then the email had been doomed the moment she typed it, and the apology had been equally doomed, and nothing she chose now mattered. But the study hadn't said jokes always failed. It said writers were overconfident about them, which was different. That left a gap, a space where her next move still counted for something, and she found she preferred the gap to the certainty.

Deckard replied on Saturday with two lines: thanked her, said the new watering schedule was posted, and asked if she could close on Sunday. She said yes, and hated a little how quickly she acceded, how the yes had arrived before she'd decided anything. Closing meant missing the bonfire at Ronan's cousin's place, the last one before everyone scattered to colleges. She told herself it was a professional trade, goodwill for a schedule, and told herself also that this was exactly the kind of thing people said when they were losing something and wanted a receipt for it.

At closing on Sunday she found a note on the register in Deckard's blocky handwriting: "Cactus shelf, once a week, not more." Underneath, smaller, he had added, "I looked up your study." Amy read it three times. She watered the outdoor beds, swept the aisles, counted the drawer twice because the first count came out wrong, and locked up under a sky going amber at the edges. On the walk home she could still hear the bonfire, faintly, a few streets over, someone laughing at something she hadn't heard. She kept walking, and then she stopped, and stood in the middle of the sidewalk listening until the laugh came again.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word diploma comes from a Greek word meaning "paper folded double," from the earlier practice of folding official documents.
story:
The chairs had been set up on the football field in rows so straight they looked drawn with a ruler, and by eleven the sun had already turned the grass to a smell of cut hay and hot metal. Parker sat between Simon and Florent, both of them sweating through their gowns, and did not look at either of them. He and Simon had not spoken in nine days, not since the argument in the parking lot, and the ceremony was too long and too public a place to keep that up.

"Nice day for it," Florent said, to the air between them.

"Sure," Parker said.

The principal was saying something about journeys. Parker's father sat in the fourth row of the family section with his leg propped on a folding chair beside him, the brace visible under his khaki pants where the surgery scar ran. He had insisted on coming. He had also insisted, that morning, that Parker not say anything to the guidance office about the deferral forms still sitting unsigned in the kitchen drawer.

Simon leaned forward to see around Parker toward Florent. "Tell him the thing," Simon said.

"There's no thing."

"There is a thing. My mom heard it from his mom." Simon's jaw worked. He had wanted, for four months, the two of them sharing a dorm room at State, had planned it down to which side of the room got the window, and now he wanted it said out loud where Parker couldn't slide away from it. "Tell him you're not coming."

The row in front of them turned around. Parker kept his eyes on the stage, where Mr. Wijaya was crossing to the podium to read names, his voice steady and unhurried as it had been all year in fifth-period history. Parker had learned more in that class than anywhere else, including the afternoon Mr. Wijaya let them waste twenty minutes arguing about where words came from, and Parker had gone home and looked up more of them, which was how he had found the one he was still carrying around.

"Woods, Parker," Mr. Wijaya said.

Parker crossed the baked grass, shook the hand offered to him, and took the leatherette folder. The sun caught the foil seal and for a second the cheap thing was transfigured, gold and serious, and then it was just a folder again in his damp grip. He walked back to his row already working at the flap with his thumb.

He opened it on his lap. The certificate inside lay flat, pristine, unfolded. He held it out to Florent without a word, tilted so Simon could see it too, and said, quietly, "It's not even folded."

"Is it supposed to be?"

"Diploma. It's from a Greek word for paper folded double. They used to fold official documents." He looked at Simon while he said it, because Simon was the one who had accused him of taking the easy way out, of hiding behind his father's leg, and Parker had spent nine days not sure whether that was true. "So I figure the folding is the point. Somebody decided this mattered, so they creased it."

Simon looked at the flat page for a long moment. "That's your answer to me? A word thing?"

"It's not an answer."

"It has to be an answer. Room assignments go in next week." Simon's voice dropped to almost nothing, friable, like it would crumble if pushed. "My whole first year, I built it around you being there. I'm not going to apologize for being mad about that."

"You don't have to apologize." Parker closed the folder. His father was watching him from the family section, half out of his chair as if he thought he might be needed, and behind him the parking lot shimmered and the whole decision sat there like a quagmire with a firm-looking crust on top: stay, defer, take the loans, move his father in with his aunt, none of the options clean. He believed, at the same time and without contradiction, that his father would manage if he left and that his father would say he was managing either way. He could not make those two beliefs agree, and he was done pretending he could.

"Mr. Wijaya," he said instead, when the line of graduates began shuffling toward the exits, "did you know about the folding?"

Mr. Wijaya considered the folder in Parker's hand. "I did not," he said, "but then, mine's been flat for thirty years."

Florent laughed, and after a second Simon did too, a short unwilling sound, and Parker put the folder under his arm where the sun couldn't get at it. His father was standing now, leaning on one cane, waiting at the gate with his hand already raised.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Consent to sexual activity must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time, including after activity has already started.
story:
The assignment had seemed simple when Mr. Ong handed it out: each group would prepare a short lesson on sexual health and deliver it to the ninth graders who were coming to visit the school in June. Daniel's group had drawn consent, contraception and testing for infections, three topics he had never once said aloud in sequence, and Carlo had already declared that he would handle the slides and nothing else. That left the actual explaining to Daniel and Ines, which was why they were sitting on the tiled porch of Daniel's grandmother's house on a Saturday afternoon, a binder open between them and a plate of biscuits going stale at their elbows.

The house belonged to his late grandfather, technically, though it had been his grandmother's domain for six years now, smelling of camphor and overbrewed tea. She had waved them through the kitchen with only a brief remonstration about shoes, and then left them alone, which Daniel appreciated, because the material was difficult enough without an audience. Ines had printed the clinic's pamphlets from the health centre downtown, and she was sorting them into piles: contraception here, testing there, consent on its own, as though the topics could be physically separated.

"The problem," Daniel said, "is that the ninth graders are going to nod at the contraception part and stare at their shoes during everything else. We can't just read facts off a page." He picked up the consent pamphlet. It was the thinnest of the three, which struck him as backwards, since it was the part people actually got wrong.

Ines suggested a role-play. She had seen one in Mr. Ong's class in the autumn, a scene set at a doctor's office, and she thought they could rebuild it from memory: a patient asking questions, a friend accompanying them, the questions getting harder as the scene went on. Carlo, who had drifted over from the slide deck at the mention of performing, immediately cast himself as the doctor and began reading the clinic pamphlet in a stethoscope voice, which made Ines laugh into her sleeve and made Daniel, despite himself, laugh too. His grandmother appeared at the screen door with fresh tea, observed them for a moment, and retreated without comment.

They worked through the contraception section first because it was the most concrete. Ines knew the clinic's hours from her cousin, who had gone for a prescription, and Daniel wrote the address and the walk-in times on an index card, then a second card explaining that appointments were confidential, that a sixteen-year-old could go without a parent, that the test for infections was mostly a urine sample or a swab and that results came back within a week. He said these sentences out loud to practise them, and hearing them in his own voice in his grandmother's quiet house made them realer than the pamphlet had.

Then they reached the hard part. Carlo, still in his doctor voice, invented a patient question on the spot, the kind Mr. Ong had warned them the ninth graders might actually ask. Say a person said yes to something earlier in the evening, the patient asked. Does that yes cover whatever happens after? Can a person just take it back in the middle, once things have started, or is that unfair to the other person?

The porch went quiet except for the cicadas. Daniel started to answer and found he was reaching for something he had never put into words, only absorbed from half-remembered assemblies and a poster in the corridor he had walked past a hundred times. He knew the shape of it. He tried it anyway, slowly. "Consent has to be freely given," he said. "And it can be withdrawn at any time, even after the activity has already started." Saying it aloud, he understood for the first time that the second half was the part that mattered, the part that changed everything, because a yes given at nine o'clock was not a contract that held until morning.

Carlo pushed back, because that was Carlo's role in every group project. Isn't it axiomatic, he asked, that once you agree to something you follow through? You don't get to withdraw from a football match at halftime because you feel like it. Ines pointed out that a football match was a bad comparison and that people were not teams, and the two of them argued about it while Daniel sat with his hand flat on the consent pamphlet, thinking about a party last spring where a friend of a friend had cried in the bathroom and nobody had asked the right question. He had not been involved. He had not known what to call what he half-knew. He knew now, or at least he had the sentence for it.

"It's not unfair," Daniel said finally, when they had wound down. "That's the whole point of it being freely given. If the other person keeps going after someone withdraws, that's not sex anymore, it's assault." Carlo opened his mouth, then closed it, and wrote something in the margin of the script without arguing further. Ines looked at Daniel with an expression he could not fully read, something between surprise and approval, and said they should keep that exact phrasing for the presentation.

His grandmother called them in at dusk for noodles, and over the meal she asked what the binder was for, since she had watched them bent over it all afternoon. Daniel said it was for a health presentation, and when she asked which part was giving them the most trouble, he hesitated, weighing how much a woman of her generation would want to hear. But she had raised four children and outlived a husband, and she only said, "The part where people change their minds, I expect. That part has always been the difficult one," and went back to her soup as though the provenance of the lesson were obvious and unremarkable.

Later, walking Ines and Carlo to the gate while the moths circled the porch light, Daniel thought about whether he would say the sentence to the ninth graders with the same certainty he had found on the porch, or whether certainty would fail him in front of thirty faces. He suspected some of them would push back the way Carlo had, and he suspected he would not have tidy answers for everything, only the one fact, held out flat like an index card. He locked the gate behind them and stood a moment in the dark, still holding the key.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
Rosalie stood in the east hallway with her gown half unzipped, holding her cap in one hand and a strip of tape in the other, because the tassel had come loose during the group photo and nobody had scissors. Kathy was taping name cards to lockers, a thing the student council had invented called the Senior Wall, which was really just lockers with paper on them. "You're putting yours crooked," Rosalie said. "You always hang things crooked. Your bedroom posters look like a ransom note."

"They look avant-garde," Kathy said. "There's a difference, and it's confidence."

Remy came down the hall carrying two trays of cupcakes from the party room, which had run out of table space, and set them on the floor beside the trophy case. He was already eating one, which Rosalie felt violated some rule of catering, though she said nothing. Through the open gym doors she could hear the party, the dj, her classmates' parents pretending to dance. She looked down the row of lockers, all those names in Kathy's slanted handwriting, and something snagged in her mind, the way a sleeve catches on a door handle. She walked the row slowly, reading.

"Where's Desmond's card?" she asked. "And Priya. She started with us, grade nine, she sat behind me in English." There were others, she realized, standing there with tape she'd stopped using. Marcus, who'd been there until junior year and then just wasn't, the way a chair is there and then isn't, no announcement. She counted the cards, then counted again differently, trying to remember who had walked in on the first day of grade nine, four years ago, when the hallway had smelled like fresh wax and everyone's shoes were too new.

"Mr. Zhao," she called, because he was passing with a folding chair under each arm, the way he always carried them, like a man transporting reluctant animals. "Do you know how many kids graduated with us versus how many started?"

He set the chairs down. "You could look it up, it's public. I will say no more, because if I start explaining statistics at a party your mother will have me removed." He picked up the chairs and went on toward the gym, humming.

She found the number on her phone, leaning against the lockers with her cap on the floor between her feet: the US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year. She read it twice. Thirteen out of every hundred, gone somewhere. She had never thought of herself as part of a cohort, which sounded like a word for Roman soldiers, and it struck her that she'd been carrying two ideas that didn't touch. One was hers: graduation as a personal finish line, hers alone, a door she'd pushed through by will. The other was the number's: graduation as something that happened to a whole age group at once, unevenly, and the unevenness was the part nobody put on banners. She didn't know how to hold both. The hallway felt simultaneously like a place she had earned and a place she'd been lucky to still be standing in, and she could not make those collapse into one clean feeling, though she suspected the honest position was somewhere uncomfortable in between.

"There you are," Remy said, appearing with a cupcake held out like a peace offering. "You have the face you get in physics when the problem has two right answers."

"Eighty-seven percent," she said. "The national average graduation rate, public schools, 2021-22. Adjusted cohort, which means the kids who started ninth grade with you, tracked all the way through." She showed him the screen. "We're the eighty-seven. Desmond's the other thirteen, kind of. Not exactly, it's an average, it's not our school, but you see it."

"So we're lucky," Remy said.

"Or we worked hard. Or both. I genuinely don't know which, and I think pretending I do is the lazy answer." She picked up her cap. "I used to think it was all me. Then for a second I thought it was all luck, which felt worse but also kind of exhilarating, honestly, like stepping off a curb you didn't know was there." She laughed at herself. "The truth's probably some ugly fraction I can't reduce."

"That's the most incisive thing anyone's said today, and today a valedictorian quoted Nietzsche." He pointed the cupcake at the Senior Wall. "So what do we do, become statisticians?"

"We write the other names down." She pulled a fresh card and a marker from Kathy's box. She wrote Desmond's name in her own even, uninteresting handwriting and taped it to the locker beside hers, straight. Then Priya's. Then Marcus's, spelled the way he'd spelled it on the seating chart, with the u nobody used. It wasn't a solution to anything, she knew that. It was paper and tape in a hallway that would be stripped bare by Monday. But she kept writing, and behind them the party went on, and Kathy came back with more tape and asked what they were doing.

"Arbitrage," Rosalie said. "Kathy hangs the cards crooked, I hang them straight. Between us we average out."

Kathy looked at the three new names, and the tape dispenser stalled in her hand for a moment before she clicked it. "Give me the marker," she said.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: By the JavaBeans naming convention, a getter for a field named 'score' is called getScore(), and a getter for a boolean field is usually named with 'is', like isActive().
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and burnt solder, and Jayden had been staring at the same forty lines of code for eleven minutes. Their robot had passed inspection that morning, but the scoring tablet refused to display anything except zero, and the first practice match began in half an hour. Milo sat beside him on the bleachers with the laptop tilted between them, chewing a pen cap and occasionally scrolling without asking.

"Try printScore," Milo said.

Jayden scrolled again. "It's not called that. Look." He pointed at the class Milo had written on the bus the night before, a private int field named score and then a method named fetchResult, another called sendPoints, and something called grabVal that returned a double nobody could account for. "You named every getter something different."

"They all work," Milo said, which was true in the way that a drawer full of unlabeled keys all opens something. Jayden knew that his own code was neater, his father's old truism about a place for everything ringing in his head whenever he opened a project, but neatness had never won them a match. Their old code had been tidy and slow. Milo's was fast and illegible.

Lorelai arrived with two paper cups of vending machine hot chocolate and set one on the bleacher beside Jayden, careful of the keyboard. She had transferred in from a team whose sponsors were, as she put it, spectacularly impecunious, so she was used to fixing things with whatever was at hand. "What's broken?"

"The display," Jayden said. "The robot's sending the score fine. The tablet just can't find the method."

She leaned in, read for a moment, and then sat back. "At my old school we used the JavaBeans convention. A getter for a field named score is just called getScore. And if the field is a boolean, you usually name it with is, like isActive."

Milo frowned at his own code. "So there's a rule?"

"It's a convention," she said. "Not enforced. Just what everybody expects."

Jayden thought about that while the announcer tested the microphone two courts over, the words booming and then thinning into the echo of the gym. A rule that nobody enforced was a strange kind of rule, but he could see the shape of it, the way it let a stranger read your code like a street with signs instead of a street with none.
