He wanted to argue that Milo's names carried more information, that sendPoints told you something getScore didn't, but in the eleven minutes of staring he had learned exactly nothing from those names, and he knew it. Still, he didn't want to just overwrite Milo's work while Milo sat there. That was a way of saying your half of the bus ride didn't count.

"Can I refactor it?" he asked. "Rename them all, keep the logic."

Milo took the pen cap out of his mouth. "It's my code."

"It's our robot."

They held that for a second, and Jayden realized he was doing the thing he hated when adults did it to him, externalizing a disagreement as if it were a technical necessity rather than a request. He tried again. "I want to. Not because your names are wrong. Because we have twenty minutes and I can't read them."

Milo exhaled through his nose, almost a laugh, and slid the laptop across. "Fine. But I'm watching."

Jayden worked fast. score got its getScore, and he found the boolean field Milo had buried in the arm controller and gave it isActive, saying the name out loud as he typed it so Milo could hear how ordinary it sounded. Lorelai read over his shoulder and caught one he missed, a boolean named up that he renamed isUp, and they argued pleasantly about whether that was ugly until they agreed it was ugly and correct, which settled it.

With four minutes left, he wrote a small test class in the corner of the file, three lines that made a new object, called getScore, and printed whatever came back. He had never written a test before. He ran it before the match, not sure whether he expected it to pass, and the console printed 12, which was right, which meant the tablet would read it too. Milo clapped his shoulder once, hard, and Lorelai collected the cups.

The practice match went badly in every way that had nothing to do with code; the arm clipped the platform and a wheel came loose and the score on the tablet, faithful now, climbed to 14 and stayed there. Afterward, in the pit area, Jayden opened the file again and looked at the test he'd written, then at the empty space below it, wondering how many of these a real program needed, and whether you ever knew when you had enough. Ms. Jung passed behind them with a clipboard and said, "Queue three, nine minutes," and Milo was already tightening the wheel, and Jayden started typing.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
story:
The thermomter read 135 when Carson pulled the roast off the grill, exactly the number his mother had written on the folded paper in her neat pharmacist's handwriting, and for one whole minute he stood in the smoke feeling like a magistrate who had just handed down a correct verdict. Then he set the meat on the cutting board his father used for fish, and the board sat there in the firelight while he went to check the rice.

"You're staring at it," Kaydence said from the picnic table. She had come over from the next site with her paperback and her dying headlamp, ostensibly to help, actually to escape her little brother. "It's a roast. It can't feel you staring."

"It looks done," Carson said. "It looked done at 130, honestly."

Zak crouched by the cooler and extracted the last soda with the ceremony of a man retrieving evidence. "My uncle pulled a pork loin off at exactly the right temp last summer and it came out like shoe leather. Everybody ate it anyway and said nothing, which was somehow worse." He popped the tab. "Nobody could figure it out. He had the thermometer. He checked it like four times."

Carson looked at the roast again. The site was quiet except for the creek and the loop of kayaks settling on the roof of the Suburban. His parents had taken the twins on the twilight ranger talk and would be back within the hour, and the whole point of tonight, the thing he had argued for on the drive up, was that he could handle dinner. He was eighteen. He was leaving for college in eleven days. His mother had said "if you're sure" in the tone she used when she was deciding whether to be sure on his behalf.

"It keeps cooking," he said slowly, mostly to himself. "Off the heat. I read that somewhere. It's called carryover cooking. A big roast can climb several more degrees after you pull it."

Zak pointed his soda at him. "Then your uncle's a solved case."

"But I took it out right at the target." Carson picked up the thermometer, wiped it, slid it back into the thickest part of the roast the way his mother had shown him, at an angle, avoiding the fat. The display blinked and settled: 138. He watched it long enough to see the last digit tick to 139. The meat was still climbing toward overdone while he stood there holding the evidence in his hand, and there was nothing to do about it now except learn the shape of the mistake.

"Take it off earlier next time," Kaydence said. "That's the whole trick, isn't it. You have to pull it before it's where you want it."

He had been circumspect about the whole evening, following the paper's instructions to the letter, refusing Zak's offer to "improvise a rub," and now he understood that his care had been aimed at the wrong moment. The instructions were true and the instructions had failed him, or rather he had failed to ask when the instructions stopped being true. He carved the end piece and tasted it: not shoe leather, but past the pink his mother liked, the lean edge already beginning to desiccate along the grain. The middle was still fine. He arranged the slices with the good ones on top.

Headlights swept the pines. The twins came down the path first, shouting something about a screech owl, and then his mother, and then his father carrying a sleeping child against his shoulder. Carson felt the old impulse to narrate his success before anyone asked, and swallowed it.

"How's the roast?" his mother said, washing her hands at the pump, and he told her the truth: that he had pulled it at the number she gave him and the number had been wrong, or the timing of the number had, that it had kept cooking on the board and gone past where she liked it. He said the middle was still good. He said he'd know for next time.

She dried her hands on her shorts and looked at him for a moment longer than the statement seemed to require. Then she took a slice from the middle, ate it standing up, and said, "Pull it at 125, then, for a roast this size. You figure that out yourself?"

"Mostly Zak's uncle," Carson said.

Zak raised his soda in acknowledgment from the fire's edge, where he was toasting a marshmallow with more ambition than technique. The twins were claiming plates. Kaydence had drifted back toward her own site, paperback under her arm, and paused at the edge of the light.

"You're going to cook for yourself in eleven days," she called back to him. "You know that, right?"

Carson set out the last clean plate for his father, who was still standing in the dark with the sleeping child, swaying slightly, unwilling to put him down and end the night. "Yeah," Carson said. "Pull it early."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Murmansk, a Russian port north of the Arctic Circle, stays ice-free all year because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current.
story:
The trail switchbacked up through pines until the trees thinned and the ridge opened onto a view of the valley, grey-green and folding away toward a horizon that suggested, without showing it, the sea. Riley carried the laminated current map rolled in his back pocket like a permit he hadn't earned yet. Tomorrow morning, third period, he had to stand in front of Mr. Villanueva's class and explain how warm water moving north across the Atlantic keeps northern Europe warmer than it had any right to be, and so far every attempt he'd made at his desk had collapsed into the word "somehow."

Alena had proposed the hike. She claimed the trail would help him learn it, though she also admitted she wanted to see the fire tower before the light went, and they had maybe three hours before the park gate closed at dusk. That was the real clock, not the exam. The exam was abstract; the gate was germane in a way an exam never managed to be. She set a fast pace up the switchbacks and called quiz questions over her shoulder.

"Why is Lisbon warmer than New York, roughly, at the same latitude?"

"Wind off warm water. The current." He unrolled the map against his thigh without breaking stride. The arrows coiled across the Atlantic like handwriting he was only partly literate in, and he suspected Alena knew more than she was saying, because her father worked on container ships and she had grown up hearing about ports the way other kids heard about highway exits.

At the fire tower they sat on the lowest step of the rusted stairs and shared a thermos. Riley spread the map across both their knees, weighting the corners with pebbles, because the wind coming up the valley wanted it. "Okay," he said. "Here's the Gulf Stream, off the east coast of the U.S., and it carries warm water north and east. Past here it becomes the North Atlantic Current, and that water spreads toward Europe." He traced it twice, the second time slower. The arrows weren't decoration, he realized; they were the thing itself, a way of making something invisible hold still long enough to be argued with. The map didn't just represent the current, it practically reified it, turned a moving idea into an object you could hold and defend or be wrong about.

"So explain Murmansk," Alena said.

"Where?"

She pointed at the upper corner of the map, where the coastlines ran off the edge of the print. "My dad's ship called there in January. Russian port, north of the Arctic Circle. Explain why he didn't need an icebreaker."

Riley stared at the map. He wanted to say it couldn't be true, that a port that far north should be locked in ice all winter, and he almost said so, which was exactly the kind of thing he would have said in class tomorrow if she hadn't asked here first. Instead he followed the arrows again, up past the British Isles, north and east, his finger running off the printed edge toward where Murmansk had to be. "It stays ice-free all year," he said slowly, "because of warm water carried by the North Atlantic Current." He heard how it sounded, flat as a fact read off a card, and he didn't yet know whether he believed it or was only repeating it, but the arrows pointed there, and the arrows pointed there for a reason.

"Say the last part again but like you mean it," Alena said, and he did, and the second time it was his own sentence.

They were halfway down, moving fast through the blue dusk, when he tried the whole explanation aloud, start to finish, and heard where it went thin. He could draw the flow and name the ports and even say why his grandmother's village in Norway had a harbor, but when he tried to go past the warm water into what warmth actually did when it arrived, he ran out of map. "I can't explain the mechanism," he admitted. "I know the current goes there, I know Murmansk doesn't freeze, and I can't tell you a single thing about why beyond that. Tomorrow I'm going to have to stand there and say that out loud." He was surprised by how much it bothered him, and by how much better the honest version sounded than the somehow he'd been rehearsing.

"The gate closes in forty minutes," Alena said, and started to run, and Riley ran after her with the map still rolled in his pocket, holding it with one hand so it wouldn't work loose.

fact: On May 9, 2013, the daily average carbon dioxide level measured at Mauna Loa passed 400 parts per million for the first time in the record.
story:
Henry had spread his science notes across the picnic table in the backyard like a dealer laying out cards, and so far the deck was winning. The graph was the worst of it: a red line climbing in a shallow, patient curve across a century, with a dashed line at four hundred parts per million that the red line crossed somewhere in the middle-right of the page, as casually as a hiker stepping over a stream.

"Explain it to me again," said Nyah, who was lying in the grass with her sunglasses on despite the overcast sky, "but this time like I'm a person, not a textbook."

"You are a person. That's the problem. People want stories." Henry tapped the graph. "Okay. Sunlight comes in, that's easy, sunlight just comes in. The Earth warms up and radiates heat back out, except greenhouse gases sit there like a blanket and keep some of the heat from leaving. More gas, thicker blanket."

"A blanket," Nyah said. "See, that I can work with. Blanket, good. Very cosmopolitan of you, explaining things with household objects."

"That is not what cosmopolitan means."

"It could be."

From the other side of the fence came the sound of a screen door, and Ms. Mendoza appeared in her own backyard with a watering can and an expression that suggested she had been listening for some time. She was the sort of neighbor who knew everyone's exam schedule and had opinions about the grass. "Is that the carbon dioxide one," she called over the fence, pointing her watering can at the graph. "My granddaughter showed me that picture. The line that goes up. It crosses the four hundred somewhere, doesn't it."

"It does," Henry said. "Four hundred parts per million. First time in the whole record."

"And what year was that?"

Henry opened his mouth and discovered, with the particular horror of a student who has studied everything except the thing being asked, that he did not know. "Nineteen," he began, and then heard himself say, "ninety-eight?"

Nyah lifted her sunglasses to look at him the way one looks at a dog that has just walked into a sliding door. Makenna, who had been quietly eating chips at the end of the table and following the conversation like a tennis match, lowered the bag. "You said the exam was Thursday," she said. "You said you were ready."

"I am ready. I'm ready on mechanisms. Dates are just, dates are furniture."

"Furniture," said Ms. Mendoza, with enormous enjoyment. "In my day we called them facts." She set down the watering can, which was a bad sign, and leaned on the fence. "I'll tell you what. You find out the real answer, and you come tell me. I've been wondering since my granddaughter showed me. If you get it wrong twice, I want to hear the right one anyway, because I intend to repeat it at book club and I refuse to be wrong at book club."

So now it was a matter of honor, or at least of book club. Henry went inside, found his laptop balanced on the picnic table between a soda can and Nyah's elbow, and searched. It took ninety seconds, which felt simultaneously too long and embarrassingly short.

"May ninth," he said. He made himself enunciate it clearly, because he was not going to mumble his redemption. "Twenty thirteen. On May 9, 2013, the daily average carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa passed four hundred parts per million for the first time in the record."

"Mauna Loa," repeated Ms. Mendoza. "Where's that?"

"Hawaii. There's an observatory on the volcano. They've been measuring up there since the fifties because the air is clean and it's far from cities, so the reading is the whole planet's, basically, not just one town's."

"The whole planet's number," Ms. Mendoza said slowly, as if tasting it. "Measured on a volcano in Hawaii. That's very cosmopolitan."

"That is STILL not what it means," Henry said, and Nyah made a small triumphant sound from the grass.

Makenna pulled the graph toward her and ran her finger along the curve. "Here's what I don't get. It wiggles. Every year it goes up and down a little, like teeth, and then up and down again. Why the teeth?"

Henry looked at the wiggles. He had memorized the shape without ever letting himself wonder about it, the way you can know a friend's face without being able to say what shape their eyebrows are. "I don't actually know," he said. "I could guess. Plants? There's more land in the northern half of the planet, so maybe in northern summer the plants breathe in more and the number dips, and in winter it climbs back. But that's a guess, and I'd want to check before I said it in an exam."

"That's the first honest thing you've said all afternoon," said Nyah.

"It's the first honest thing I've said all semester. The rest was confidence."

Ms. Mendoza had picked up her watering can again, but she hadn't gone inside. She looked at the graph for a while, at the little sawtooth rise of it, at the dashed line it had crossed in 2013 and kept climbing past without pause or apology. "You know what that line is," she said at last. "It's an indictment. Quiet, no shouting, just going up. In court I'd say that's the worst kind of witness, one that never stops talking and never raises its voice."

She watered a row of tomatoes that did not appear to need it. "Book club Thursday," she said. "Seven o'clock. You can tell them the Hawaii part yourself, and if Sandy argues, you tell her a boy with a blanket explained it to you."

Henry folded the graph carefully, sawtooths and all, and slid it into his folder between the notes he trusted and the notes he'd have to check. Nyah rolled over, pushed her sunglasses up into her hair, and said, "Blanket, teeth, volcano. Honestly, if the exam is anything like this afternoon, you're fine."

"Unless they ask me a date."

"Then point at Makenna."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced the five stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance in her 1969 book On Death and Dying, originally to describe terminally ill patients facing their own death.
story:
The windshield wipers had a rhythm Mia could not stop counting, two seconds on, one off, while her father drove them back from the funeral home through rain the color of dishwater. Her grandfather's glasses case sat in the cupholder between the seats because nobody knew what else to do with it, and her mother kept looking at it and then away.

"You're very quiet," her mother said.

"I'm fine."

"She's fine," her father repeated, to the road.

Mia scrolled her phone. Aryan had texted three times, the last one reading, you don't have to feel anything, you know, and she had not answered because she did not know if that was true. In Ms. Ricci's class in the spring they had done a unit on grief, and Ms. Ricci had handed out a diagram shaped like a staircase: denial, then anger, then bargaining, then depression, then acceptance, five tidy steps with arrows between them. Mia had copied it into her notebook and underlined it twice, the way she underlined things she expected to need later. Now she sat in the back seat of the car with her grandfather eleven hours dead and felt none of it. She was not in denial; nobody had let her be. She was not angry. She had caught herself, during the eulogy, thinking about a parking ticket, and had felt like something was wrong with her rather than with the staircase.

She typed the five stages into the search bar, mostly to prove to herself that she had remembered the order.

Her mother turned around at a red light. "What are you doing back there?"

"Looking something up."

"Not at the service. At the service, put it away."

"We left the service, Mom. Twenty minutes ago."

Her father's hands shifted on the wheel. "Let her look something up."

The article loaded. It was longer than she expected, and she read it twice, because the first time she thought she had misread. Kübler-Ross, 1969, On Death and Dying. She had assumed the book was about mourners, about people like her in cars with a dead grandfather's glasses case, but the first line said the stages described terminally ill patients facing their own death. Dying people, not the ones left behind. She read it a third time to test its veracity, because a thing on the internet could be wrong, and this felt like the kind of thing somebody would get wrong and pass around until it was everywhere.

"Aryan says hi," she said, buying time.

"Tell Aryan we're sorry she couldn't come," her mother said, and turned back around.

Mia checked a second source, then a third. They agreed. The five stages, the ones Ms. Ricci had drawn as arrows on the whiteboard, had been introduced in 1969 by Elisabeth Kübler-Ross in her book On Death and Dying, and she had written them originally to describe the responses of dying patients to their own dying. Mia sat with that. It was not that the model was useless. Her grandfather, in the hospice in March, had said it's not my time, and later, tell God I'll quit smoking, which the nurses had let stand as a joke though everyone in the room understood it was not one. He had climbed Ms. Ricci's staircase. She, in the back seat, had climbed nothing.

"Can I say something weird," she said.

"Is it about the will," her father said, "because we are not doing the will today."

"It's not about the will." She leaned forward between the seats. "You know those five stages everybody talks about? Denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance."

"From your psychology class," her mother said. "I remember."

"They were for the person dying. That's who Kübler-Ross wrote about. Not the family after. Her book was On Death and Dying, 1969, and the stages described terminally ill patients facing their own death." She heard herself delivering it like a citation and stopped. "I keep waiting to feel the steps. I don't feel any of them."

Her father took the exit ramp too fast and the glasses case slid against the cupholder with a small clack. "So what do you feel?"

"Nothing, mostly. I keep checking and it's just quiet in there. Quiescent." She had used the word in an essay once and her grandfather, reading over her shoulder, had said, quiescent, look at you, college words, and she had to grip the seat now, briefly, before she could keep talking. "So either I'm broken, or the map was drawn for somebody else's country."

Her mother's voice went careful, the voice she used at funerals. "You can't abrogate your feelings by finding a technicality, Mia."

"That's not what I'm doing." But she checked herself, because it was a little what she was doing, or close to it. "Or maybe it is. Maybe I want a reason it's okay that I'm not crying. But it's also true. She wrote it about the dying. Somebody turned it into a rule for everybody else, and then teachers hand it out, and people like me sit in cars feeling defective."

The rain thinned. Her father signaled and pulled into the cemetery access road, which they had to take to reach the highway, and for a hundred yards the rows of stones moved past the windows, gray and wet and patient. Nobody spoke. Mia looked at her mother's hand on the armrest, at the ring her grandfather had given her grandmother, which her mother had inherited decades early now.

"There's no schedule," her father said finally. "Your grandmother didn't cry for a month when her sister died, and then she couldn't stop for a week. Nobody handed her a staircase."

"Grandpa told me that once," Mia said. "About Nonna."

"He would have." Her father's jaw worked. "He liked the messy ones."

They came out on the highway and the wipers, sensing the lighter rain, slowed to their longer interval, and the sound Mia had been counting became something she could let go of. She texted Aryan: it's not a checklist, it was never for us. Then, before sending, she deleted it, because she was not sure that was the conclusion either, only that she was allowed not to know yet. She pocketed the phone. The glasses case sat in its cupholder, keeping whatever it was keeping, and her father drove, and at some point the sun found one clean stripe through the clouds and laid it across the windshield like a hand.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Starting with applicants for 2026 entry, UCAS replaced the free-form personal statement with three structured questions about why the applicant wants the subject and how they have prepared.
story:
Olivier had claimed the table by the window on the second floor of the library, the one with the wobbly leg he had learned to steady with a folded receipt, because from there he could see the whole car park and the bare plane tree, and if the email came while he was watching, he would feel somehow more equal to it. His laptop was open to his inbox. It had been open to his inbox for two hours.

Megan dropped into the opposite chair without asking, peeling off her scarf. "Still nothing?"

"Still nothing. It could be weeks. It could be tonight. Nobody tells you which."

"That's barbaric." She unwrapped a sandwich and, before he could object, slid half across the table to him. "Eat something. You look like the plane tree."

He took a bite because refusing Megan's food was more effort than eating it. Between them, half-eaten, lay his printed application, the pages soft from being thumbed so many times. The truth was he had begun to distrust the thing, the way you distrust a map once you learn the territory has shifted.

"You know what's funny," he said. "In October I nearly submitted something completely wrong. My cousin Ravi, he applied for medicine three years ago, and he coached me. He said the personal statement is one big essay, four thousand characters, everything about you in one flowing argument, starting with a hook. He spent a whole Sunday helping me burnish it. Made my work experience at the clinic sound like a small epic. He was good at it, honestly. It read beautifully."

Megan chewed and waited, because she knew him well enough to know there was a turn coming.

"So I wrote it his way. And then Alex, who was over at mine revising, looked at the form and said, why are you typing one essay, there are three boxes. Three questions." He laughed, quietly, because the library's second floor had its own etiquette and its own enforcer, a librarian with a cardigan and a stare. "From this year, for 2026 entry, they scrapped the free-form personal statement. It's three structured questions now. Why you want the subject, and how you've prepared for it, and that kind of thing. Ravi's whole system, everything he taught me, was for a form that doesn't exist anymore."

"That's actually tragic. All that Sunday."

"It wasn't wasted exactly. The material still existed. I had it all, the reading, the clinic, the coding project. I just had to cut it up and sort it into the right boxes instead of weaving it into one narrative. Ravi wanted the essay to be a story with a shape and a crescendo. The new form wants you to answer the question you were asked." He turned his half of the sandwich in his hands. "I spent an evening furious about it, and then I realised I couldn't decide which way was actually better. Ravi's way let you be persuasive. The new way makes everybody comparable. I still don't know which of those I believe in."

"Both, probably," Megan said. "That's the boring answer. You're allowed the boring answer."

"That's what Mr. Ross said, more or less. I went to him in October panicking, and he didn't explain anything, he just told me to read the form like an exam question. 'Answer the question asked,' he said, 'not the question you wish they'd asked.' Which is the most Mr. Ross sentence ever written." He smiled at the table. "In his lesson we'd been arguing about theocracy, whether a state founded on religious law can ever be legitimate, and he kept pushing me to state my principle instead of just criticising everyone else's. I think he was teaching us the personal statement before we knew we'd need it."

"You realise you just claimed a politics lesson was secretly about you."

"I realise that's facetious and I said it anyway."

Megan snorted, and the librarian's stare found them and lingered, and they bent over the pages in a show of scholarship. The afternoon light moved across the table. At some point Olivier stopped refreshing his inbox and actually read his own answers again, the three neat sections, and felt a small double feeling he could not have named if asked: pride in how clear it was, and grief for the long shaping argument that had nowhere to live now, the version of himself as a story with a crescendo, discarded like an old draft.

"Do you think you'd have got in easier the old way?" Megan asked. Her tone was careful, the way people are careful when they're asking for themselves too, because she was waiting on Durham.

"Maybe. Or maybe the essay way rewarded people with cousins like Ravi, people who get coached. Maybe boxes are fairer and I just hate that I liked the unfair thing." He closed the laptop lid until it clicked. "I can hold both. That's allowed, apparently."

The light on the car park had gone amber when his phone buzzed once against the table, face down, the screen throwing a pale square onto the ceiling. Olivier looked at it and did not move. Megan had gone very still, her hand halfway to her scarf.

"Whatever it is," she said, "open it at home."

"It's one line. It'll take one second." He reached out and turned the phone over, and the screen said only that a decision had been updated on his tracker, nothing more, nothing decided, and he sat there with his thumb above the link while below the window a woman locked her car and a magpie landed on the bare plane tree and looked at him sideways.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: ATP synthase works like a tiny rotary motor: protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP.
story:
The community garden behind the middle school had been Oliver's mother's idea, penance for a semester of biology he had nearly failed, though she hadn't used the word penance. She had said responsibility. Either way, Saturday mornings found him kneeling in the pea gravel between the beds, weeding around tomato plants that belonged to Ms. Joseph, the retired teacher who ran the plot assignments and apparently ran everything else in the garden too. His unit test on cellular respiration was Monday morning, third period, and he had brought his notes to the garden because staying home felt like admitting the material had beaten him there first.

The problem was not memorization. He could recite the order: glucose, glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, ATP. The problem was that the words sat in his head like the vocabulary lists he'd copied without understanding, and when Ms. Joseph quizzed him during their break, she caught it immediately. "You can say the steps," she said, handing him a tomato with a split skin, "but tell me why the mitochondria bother with all of it. What's it for?" He said energy because that was the answer on every worksheet, and she just looked at him, and he understood that the answer was a door he hadn't opened.

Orlando arrived at eleven with a cooler and no gloves, because Orlando never planned anything, including his presence in a garden he'd sworn off the week before. He had, however, been to the science museum the previous Sunday with his little cousin, and he would not stop talking about it. "There was this model," he said, crouching next to Oliver in the bed Ms. Joseph had allotted him as penance of his own, though his offense had only been truancy. "Clear plastic, about yay big." He held his hands a foot apart. "It was spinning. Like an actual motor, a little turbine, and there was a label."

From where he knelt pulling bindweed, Oliver could see Orlando's hands turning around each other, one fist circling the other, and something in his chest went strange. He put down the weeds. "What was it called? The model. The label."

From Orlando's side of the fence, the morning looked different than it had from Oliver's. Orlando had noticed, all week, the way Oliver checked his phone for the study app and then put it away without opening it, the way he'd gone quiet when Ms. Joseph asked her question. Orlando was not good at biology; he was good at watching. And he watched now as Oliver's whole posture changed, the slump straightening as if someone had threaded a wire through his spine. "ATP synthase," Orlando said. "The label said ATP synthase. There was this ramp of little balls, protons I think they said, and when the balls flowed down through the thing, part of it spun. Like water through a water wheel. And the spinning was what made the ATP. The sign said the spinning builds it."

Oliver stood up so fast he knocked his kneepad into the tomato cage. He had copied the phrase electron transport chain twenty times and it had never once occurred to him that anything in the chain moved, that the whole process was not a list but a machine. Protons flowing through the enzyme, making part of it spin, the spin building ATP. He said it back to Orlando exactly, checking each piece, and Orlando repeated it, annoyed now, "Yes, that's what I said," and Oliver laughed, the first time in two weeks, and started pacing the gravel path.

"Wait," he said. "That's the whole thing. That's why the steps exist. Glucose gets broken down step by step because the cell isn't burning it, it's loading it, pumping protons so they can flow back through and turn that motor." He was talking faster than the garden, faster than Ms. Joseph's compost schedule, faster than the Saturday he was supposed to be serving. Ms. Joseph came over with her watering can and listened without correcting him, which he took, correctly, as a kind of approval.

The cost came at the gate. Nathaniel biked up at noon with Oliver's phone charger and the news that the study group had moved to the library at one, without him, because he hadn't answered any messages. Oliver could make the group and arrive prepared for once, or he could finish the bed Ms. Joseph had marked as his for the day. He looked at the half-turned soil, dark as graphite, which Ms. Joseph insisted was an allotrope of the same carbon that was in every living thing, another fact Oliver had let pass through him unexamined until now.

He stayed two more hours. He turned the soil to the bed's igneous rock edging, and in his head the whole pathway ran like Orlando's turning fists, glucose to glycolysis to the cycle to the protons to the spinning motor to ATP, over and over, so that by the time he packed his notes the sequence was not memorized but familiar, the way a route home is familiar. He had missed the study group. He had, he suspected, missed Nathaniel's patience too, which was not infinite. Ms. Joseph locked the gate behind him and said the tomatoes would remember him. On the ride home, he pulled up beside Nathaniel at the stop sign and said, "I can explain the whole chain now. Want to hear it?" Nathaniel looked at him for a long second, then at the sky, then pedaled on without answering.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: A blood pressure reading gives two numbers in millimeters of mercury: systolic pressure when the heart beats, over diastolic pressure when the heart relaxes between beats.
story:
The cuff arrived in a cardboard box with a torn pamphlet folded underneath it, and Cameron read the pamphlet twice before he touched the machine, because Mr. Chukwu, who had lent it after his own doctor cleared him, had said only one thing at the door: "Read first. Then measure." That suited Cameron. He was the kind of person who assembled bookshelves before unpacking the screws.

In the kitchen, his grandfather sat at the table with his sleeve rolled up and an expression of patient suffering, the way he sat for the barber or the dentist. On the counter, Nathalie leaned against the fridge with a glass of orange juice, watching. She had come over to work on their health project and had stayed for this. "It's going to squeeze," Cameron warned, fastening the cuff above his grandfather's elbow the way the diagram showed.

The machine whirred, tightened, released, and printed a small slip of paper: 148 over 92, and beside the numbers, the letters mmHg. "What does that mean, one four eight over ninety two?" his grandfather asked. "Which is the bad one?"

Cameron looked at the pamphlet again. The top number, the systolic, was the pressure when the heart beat; the bottom number, the diastolic, was the pressure when the heart relaxed between beats. Both numbers were measured in millimeters of mercury, which the pamphlet abbreviated the same way the machine did. He had half-absorbed this in class, but explaining it aloud was different, like the difference between knowing a word and using it in a sentence. "They're not good and bad," he said slowly. "The top one is when your heart beats. The bottom one is when it relaxes between beats. They're two halves of the same thing."

His grandfather considered his own arm as though it had betrayed him personally. "And both mine are high." It wasn't a question. Cameron nodded and did not dress it up, because his grandfather had spent forty years at the plant and could smell a softened truth from across a room. "Both are high," Cameron said. "That's what the doctor said too, right? She wrote it down."

Nathalie set down her juice. "You know what's strange," she said. "Half our class doesn't even know what the numbers are. Keven thought it was a fraction. He asked if you could simplify it." She laughed, then caught herself. "And then some of them act like a high reading makes you a different category of person. Like it stigmatizes you. Which is ridiculous, because it's a measurement, not a character review." Cameron agreed with this more than he said. His grandfather had already gone quiet in a way Cameron recognized, the quiet of a man deciding he was now officially old.

"There's a thing called the DASH diet in here," Cameron went on, tapping the pamphlet. "And it says walking. Thirty minutes, most days. It says the numbers can come down." He was careful with the claim. He did not promise a cure, did not say by how much or by when, because the pamphlet didn't either, and he had learned in biology that a confident guess is still a guess. What he knew for certain was narrow and solid: the reading was two numbers, millimeters of mercury, one for the beat and one for the rest between beats, and the doctor had said the reading should be lower. The space between those two certainties was where the honest answer lived.

His grandfather pushed back from the table, went to the window over the sink, and stood there with his rolled sleeve still up. "Your grandmother walked every evening after her sister died," he said. "Around the block, twice. Rain or shine." He was quiet a moment. "I used to watch her from this window and think, there goes a woman keeping herself together." He turned around. "You're saying I should do the same."

"I'm saying it's on the list," Cameron said. "Walking, the diet, and measuring again. That's the whole list." He did not mention that his own grandfather was the reason the health project had suddenly mattered to him, the way a fact matters once it lives in your kitchen instead of a textbook. Nathalie pulled out her phone and started a shared note titled, in her slightly dramatic way, Operation Grandpa, and typed three items: walking, food, machine. She showed the screen to the old man, who squinted at it and grunted, which in his language was close to a signature.

"We'll do the first walk tonight," Nathalie said. "Three of us, so nobody can claim attrition and drop out quietly. It's a known tactic in our class." His grandfather looked from her to Cameron and back, and something in his shoulders loosened, not much, but enough to see.

He rolled down his sleeve, buttoned it, and took the printed slip from the table, folding it once and putting it in his shirt pocket, over the heart. "One forty eight over ninety two," he said. "Fine. Write it down. I want it on record, so we can beat it."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: In a model with two goods, one country cannot have a comparative advantage in both, because a lower opportunity cost for one good means a higher opportunity cost for the other.
story:
The bell over the door of Visser's Hardware had a particular clang, and Alicia had learned, over four months of Saturday shifts, to read the customers by it. A brisk clang meant a contractor. A hesitant clang meant someone with a sink problem and no vocabulary for it. This morning it rang brisk, and Mr. Visser appeared from the back room like a man summoned by biology.

"Alicia, register. Abram, restock the plumbing aisle. Both of you, quickly, we open in ten minutes and I have a delivery to sign for."

Alicia frowned at the assignment. "I restock faster than him, though. And I'm fine on the register."

"You are faster at both, yes." Mr. Visser said it the way other people said nice weather, already turning away. "Register."

She took her post behind the till and watched Abram wrestle a box of pipe fittings. It was true that she was faster at everything in the store, and not in a boastful way, merely the way it was true that the parking lot had potholes. Abram dropped a fitting, picked it up, held it to the light as though it might confess to being something else. She could have cleared that shelf in the time it took him to open the box. This was the problem she had carried in with her that morning, folded up alongside her economics notes in her backpack: a unit test on Monday, and a paragraph in the textbook that she had read four times without it ever quite becoming words. Something about two countries, two goods, trade. She had understood it for about ninety seconds in class, and then Rowan had asked whether one country could just be better at everything, and the teacher had smiled in that way that meant the answer was inside the question, and the understanding had drained out of her like water from a sink with a faulty washer, which the store sold, aisle nine.

By noon the shelf was done, badly, and Abram had developed a rhythm. Alicia rang up a woman buying three kinds of tape, none of which, the woman insisted, would do what she needed. Behind the till Alicia turned the morning over. If she did both jobs, the store got her speed twice, which sounded like winning twice. Mr. Visser was not a foolish man; he was, in fact, the most sagacious person she knew who also believed coupons expired on a whim. So the assignment was not an insult to Abram. It was arithmetic she could not yet see.

She tested it against the day. While Abram restocked, she sold. When he was slow at the shelf, he was, in a strange way, cheap at it, because the register, the thing he was not doing, was something he would have been worse at anyway. And she was expensive at the shelf, even being fast, because every shelf she stacked was a line of customers she wasn't moving through. Being best at everything and best placed to do one thing were not the same thing at all. She felt the two halves of the morning slide together with a small consonance, like a fitting that finally threads.

"Opportunity cost," she said aloud, to the receipt printer, which did not respond, being a receipt printer.

"Are you okay?" Abram had come up with a box of washers.

"I'm learning economics from your bad shelving."

"Rude," he said, "but continue."

"Watch. Suppose the store is two countries. I'm the country that's better at everything. Register and shelves, both. But if I do the shelves, what do I give up?" She waved a hand at the till, where a queue had briefly formed and dispersed during the morning rush. "And if you do the shelves, what do you give up? Almost nothing, because you were never going to be good at the till anyway. So the store puts me where the giving-up is biggest, and you where it's smallest." She paused, hearing it land in her own ears. "And here's the strange part. If I have the cheap shelves, the low cost there, then I have to have the expensive register. The two costs can't both lean the same way. One country can't have the advantage in both goods, because the low cost on one side is the same thing as the high cost on the other."

Abram set down the washers. "So the textbook thing. You just reified it. Out of me being slow."

"I used you as a nation."

"Honored," he said. "Sort of."

She thought about Rowan's question again, the one that had started the unraveling. Could one country be better at everything, in every sense, the way she was better at everything in the store? Yes, she decided, it could, and the trade would still make sense, which was the part that had felt like a magic trick on Monday and felt now like a Tuesday. Though she was less sure what happened when there were more than two goods, or more than two countries, or when the shelves were people and the register was a life, which was a thought she put back in her backpack for later.

The bell rang its brisk clang. Mr. Visser was still out back with the delivery, the line at the register had grown to four, and Abram was already walking toward it with the confidence of a man who had just been declared cheap.

"Stop," Alicia called. "That's my side."

fact: Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.
story:
Ms. Müller wrote the word on the board in florid looping script, temper, underlined it twice, and then delivered what Amelia privately classified as a peroration, ten minutes on the crystalline soul of cocoa butter while twenty-two students waited beside bowls of chopped chocolate that were slowly softening in the warm room. Amelia had heard the speech before, or a version of it, and had tuned most of it out. What she retained was a number, thirty-one and a half degrees, and a promise: if she got the chocolate into temper, it would set shiny and snap when broken.

The class divided into stations. Amelia partnered with Freya, who wanted to make filled shells for a mould she had brought from home, a tray of small domed cavities she planned to give to her brother for his birthday. Ryland worked at the next bench and had already begun arguing with the boy beside him about whether seeding with chopped chocolate worked better than pouring on a marble slab. He asked Amelia to adjudicate. She said she had no evidence either way, that she had tempered chocolate exactly once, and that the first attempt had gone wrong in a way she still didn't understand. This seemed to satisfy him less than a verdict would have, but he turned back to his own bench.

Amelia seeded her chocolate, stirring chopped callets into the melted mass, watching the thermometer drift down through the thirties. Freya took over the stirring while Amelia lined the mould with paper towels and read the recipe a second time. At thirty-two degrees they still had a few callets floating, so they stirred longer, and at thirty-one and a half Amelia dipped a knife blade and waited. The smear set within a couple of minutes, dull but firm. Not shiny, she thought. Probably wrong.

"Pour anyway," Freya said. "We're out of time before the bell."

Amelia poured. The chocolate ran into the cavities, and she tapped the mould on the bench to release air bubbles, the way a video she'd watched at midnight had shown. They scraped the excess off the top and set the tray on the rack by the window, where the October air came through the gap in the frame. Ms. Müller passed behind them, looked at the tray without stopping, and said nothing, which Amelia chose to read as either leniency or contempt.

Ryland's moulds released first. He upended his tray over baking paper, and his chocolates dropped out in a rattling row, each one glossy, and when he snapped one in half the sound carried across the room. Freya tried their own tray next. Nothing moved. She turned it over and shook it, and the domes stayed seated in the cavities like teeth in a jaw. One edge of the chocolate showed through a cavity, matte, with a dull grey bloom at the border where it met the plastic.

"Ours stuck," Freya said. She pried at a cavity with a fingernail.

Amelia stood with the empty bowl in her hands and went back over the sequence. The stirring, the temperature, the knife test that hadn't looked shiny. Then she looked at the window rack, at the draught, and then at the bench behind them, where a pot of another group's chocolate had been resting on the counter within arm's reach of their bowl for most of the last ten minutes. She couldn't prove anything from that. What she could do was the knife test again, properly this time, on what remained in the bowl: she tempered a small amount of fresh chocolate, tempered it carefully, watching the thermometer instead of the clock, and smeared it on a cold plate. It set fast, and it set shiny.

She said, "Tempered chocolate shrinks a little as it sets. That's why his fell out clean. That's why ours didn't. Ours was never in temper." She turned the stuck mould over once more, and the domes held. "We poured it too warm, or we cooled it wrong, or both. I can't tell which."

Freya had begun scraping the ruined chocolate out of the cavities with the edge of a spoon, collecting it back into the bowl. "Can we redo them?"

"There's twenty minutes."

They chopped, they melted, they stirred, and this time Amelia did not look up when Ryland started a speech at his bench about how his method had obviously been superior. She watched the thermometer instead, took the chocolate off the heat herself, and refused to pour until the knife test came back glossy under the window light. Freya filled the cavities, and they put the mould not on the rack by the draught but on the middle shelf of the cooler, where Ms. Müller kept the setting trays.

With four minutes left before the bell, Freya turned the mould over the baking paper. The first dome dropped out and rolled a centimetre across the sheet, shining under the fluorescent lights.
